44. It would be informative to see what happens if you perform harmonization on the vertex-wise gradients themselves.
45. Compute clustering and characteristic path length on weighted, signed networks (no binarization) to reduce circular dependency with the S-A axis. 46. The big conclusion is that the brain's functional organization develops from sensorimotor to association areas over the lifespan. Didn't we already know this? What is the profound new insight here, beyond putting a specific (and likely model-dependent) number on it?
47. The authors use totally different, complex preprocessing pipelines for the infant and adult data. How do we know that the differences we see in gradients during infancy are not simply artifacts of this? The infant and adult cohorts were preprocessed with different slice-timing, despiking, and ICA-denoise settings. Where is the direct evidence that these pipeline disparities don’t dominate the apparent “infant inflation” of gradient extremes?
48. NeuroSynth is based on meta-analysis and does not necessarily reflect direct cognitive measurements. How did you choose the specific 24 neurosynth terms you landed on out of hundreds of available terms? Did you do the analysis with multiple different sets of terms?
49. Motion is markedly higher in children, yet gradients are built before regressing mean FD.
Can you show scatterplots of gradient range versus FD by age band, or rerun the pipeline after scrubbing to equalize motion?
50. The spline in GAMLSS is capped at 5 df regardless of vertex or metric. Sharper infant transitions could be smoothed away. What happens if you raise df or use penalized thin-plate splines with GCV?
51. The K-means “lifespan phases” are accepted at face value. Where are the silhouette widths, gap statistic, or stability analysis across bin widths (e.g., 1-year vs 3-year bins)?
52. The entire developmental narrative is built on gradients extracted from age-bin mean FC matrices. Yet diffusion embedding is a highly nonlinear transform, meaning that the gradients of the mean FC do not necessarily reflect the “mean” gradients computed from individual FC. To carry out any meaningful study of a particular gradient axis, a template must be constructed, but little justification is given in the paper on the choice of this particular scheme for template derivation. Some comparison with other template schemes, perhaps using a naive full-lifespan template may help justify the strategy used in the manuscript.
53. The graph theoretic metrics are computed on the binarized row-wise 10% thresholded FC matrices while the gradients are computed with the 10% thresholded weighted FC matrices. Why were weighted implementations of characteristic path length and clustering coefficient not used and how does this impact the result?
54. In Figure 2c, it is initially unclear that what is being reported is actually the mean magnitude of the gradient within each network. This ambiguity could be resolved by plotting the trajectories of the mean gradient values (not magnitudes) and marking the maxima (and minima for networks on the negative pole).
55. Certain countries are restricted from accessing the Lifespan HCP datasets (see https://grants.nih.gov/grants/guide/notice-files/NOT-OD-25-083.html). Please confirm that the current study is compliant with the data use agreement of the NIMH Data Archive (NDA).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript integrates a vast amount of data to investigate the development of the principal cortical hierarchy over the lifespan, from 32 PMW through 80 years of age. The primary finding is that functional organization proceeds in 3 phases over the lifespan, ultimately establishing then refining the S-A axis. The authors investigate how different parameters of the gradient develop globally as well as at the network and region level as well as how the gradient development relates to functional properties (graph theoretical metrics of FC) and structural properties (distance, thickness, and “myelin”). I commend the authors for their very impressive effort in pulling together this large lifespan dataset and for the many informative analyses (both primary and sensitivity) that were included in the paper. This is truly a feat and emphasizes what is possible with modern collaborative imaging data sharing and analysis workflows. On the whole, I think this is an informative and impactful work that will be of broad interest. That said, while the dataset and breadth of analyses are impressive, there are several methodological and conceptual choices that may limit interpretability and should be clarified prior to publication. I summarize these in the comments below.
1. The authors continually refer the primary functional gradient as the S-A axis. However, the gradient itself looks quite different in Phase I vs the other phases. How do the authors determine that this principal gradient is indeed the S-A axis in all cases? Further, at least one prominent definition of the S-A axis comes from Sydnor et al. (Neuron, 2021) which defines an S-A axis based a variety of spatial maps. This definition of the axis has since been commonly used in published work. I would agree that the principal gradient derived here in the adolescents and adults looks very similar to that gradient, but the authors should comment on their criteria for determining if the result of their gradient analysis did indeed produce the “S-A axis” or something else. It would also be prudent to compare their derived axis to this other publicly available S-A axis as well as discuss the different manners in which this axis can be defined.
2. Related, there were methodological choices made in the connectome gradient analysis that require more rationale. For example, the authors set all negative correlations in the FC matrices to zero. Why was this done and why are these correlations not deemed meaningful? How does this impact the outcome? Additionally, seemingly arbitrary decisions are made about which edges to include, for example thresholding at the top 10% of positive correlations without explanation. The authors should must describe how and why these choices were made and how these choices impact the outcomes. This is critical as these choices may bias results in ways that differ substantially by age—especially when the age-range spans from a newborn brain and an 80 year old brain. For example, it is possible that the distribution of positive and negative correlations varies substantially across the lifespan which would feed forward into downstream analyses.
3. The analysis of how functional connectivity itself influences gradient development is an important one, particularly since the gradients are themselves based on the same FC data matrices. The focus on segregation and integration makes sense conceptually, but the reliance on graph theoretical properties to define segregation and integration abstracts the data quite a bit, and those results were the least clear. The graph theoretical approach taken here to look at segregation and integration imposes analysis decisions that may obscure informative patterns in the FC data (e.g. threshold FC matrices, binarizing values to remove variability in FC strength). This approach may miss interesting patterns that are dependent on the nuances of segregation and integration among different pairs of connections and communities (for example different combinations of changes in within and between network connectivity could potentially give rise to a similar overall integration and integration score). Recent work (e.g. Pines et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2024, both in Nature Communications) highlights how a more fine grained approach that looks at differences in FC strength more directly can yield important insights into the establishment and embedding of the cortical hierarchy. Given the prominence and highly related nature of these recent studies, the authors should consider adding a parallel approach to their investigation of FC differences underlying gradient development in the present work. At minimum, they should contextualize their findings in relation to this recent work, which is notably absent from the current manuscript references.
4. The examination of the structural properties that may contribute to gradient development is a strength of the paper. I have a minor comment that the authors are overly narrow in their labelling of the T1/T2 ratio as “myelin” or “myeloarchitecture” per se. Of course, this ratio measure is sensitive to myelin differences, but it is also sensitive to anything else that may influence T1 and T2 relaxation times, which could be a myriad of things over this wide developmental span. As such, the authors should avoid labelling differences in T1/T2 effects as differences in “myelin” specifically. This work would be equally as impactful if they simply refer to these effects as differences in T1/T2 contrast ratio and then discuss the factors that could drive this signal.
5. Related to the findings on geometric distance, the authors claim that “These findings suggest that while geometric constraints strongly influence the functional hierarchy, their influence gradually diminishes during development, potentially facilitating increased functional flexibility.” The last part of this conclusion “facilitating increased functional flexibility” bears more scrutiny and explanation. How was this conclusion drawn and how might diminishing influence of geometric distance influence functional flexibility?
6. Minor: Lines 309-310. The text states “Regional clustering analysis (Cp-node) revealed a progressive decline in spatial topography from primary to transmodal association regions. What does a decline in spatial topography mean in this context? This phrasing could be clarified.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This is a well-written and timely study that leverages a large neuroimaging dataset across a wide age range (32 postmenstrual weeks to 80 years), addressing an important question regarding the development of the cortical functional hierarchy (sensorimotor-association axis). The sample size and cross-site design are impressive. The identification of developmental shifts in the S-A gradient across the lifespan nicely summarizes recent findings and further extends them by investigating associations with cortical thickness, area expansion, myelination, functional integration and segregation, as well as cognition. I have several comments for the authors to consider:
• The S-A gradient has been shown to account for an increasing proportion of variance in the functional connectome from childhood to adulthood, and it is not consistently the dominant gradient across development (Lariviere et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2021; Dong et al., 2021). Since the current study spans the full lifespan, it would be valuable to examine how the explained variance of the S-A gradient (and the ordering of dominant vs. secondary gradients) shifts across developmental stages.
• This study identified age-related shifts in the S-A gradient consistent with previous findings, especially during early development. The authors propose an interesting idea that this shift is likely driven by increasing functional specialization and the strengthening of long-range connections. Could the authors provide direct evidence supporting this hypothesis?
• Given that network configuration (e.g., size and distribution) changes over development (Sun et al., 2025, Nature Neuroscience, from the same research group), it is unclear why the authors opted to use the adult Yeo 7-network configuration to calculate segregation and integration. Would age-specific network definitions yield more accurate estimates? I noticed that the functional segregation growth rates reported here (Fig. 3c) and those in Sun et al. (2025) appear to differ. Could the use of age-specific network configurations help explain this discrepancy?
• A related point: the spatial distribution of the S-A gradient changes across the lifespan, transitioning from an anterior–posterior configuration in prenatal/neonatal stages to a mature axis spanning somatomotor/visual to default mode regions. Could the authors elaborate further on how the topographic organization of the S-A gradient relates to age-related changes in network topology?
• Fig. 3d appears to show that integration growth also aligns with the S-A axis (e.g., increased integration in the default mode network and decreased integration in somatomotor regions). However, only a weak association was reported between the growth axis of integration and the S-A gradient (r = 0.19). Could the authors discuss this finding further?
• The authors performed Procrustes rotation for cross-subject/cross-age comparisons. Since the raw gradient may reflect individual or age-specific patterns, it would be helpful if the authors could provide the extent and effect of the rotation procedure? For example, how much rotation was applied to align the S-A gradient across individuals and age groups?
Minor
• Fig. 1c: The meaning of “dimension 1” and “dimension 2” is unclear and may be confused with the gradient dimensions. Please define these explicitly.
• Fig. 5a: The meaning of “z-stat % (max = 15)” and the labels “25, 50, 100” are unclear.
• Some sites appear to include longitudinal data. How were longitudinal data handled in the analysis?
• Please clarify the abbreviation “rm-ANOVA” as “repeated-measures ANOVA.”

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We sincerely thank the editor and all the reviewers for their comments on our manuscript, titled “Spatiotemporal dynamics of the human cortical functional hierarchy across the lifespan” (ID: NCOMMS-25-33712-T). We found the comments to be constructive and highly valuable for improving our manuscript, which we revised based on the comments received. Our point-by-point responses to the reviewers’ comments are presented below.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
In this paper, the author maps the development of the sensory-association (SA) gradients across the human lifespan and explores how these gradients relate to structural brain measures. While the characterization of the SA gradient is a valuable contribution to understanding brain organization and maturation, I have major concerns regarding several aspects of the study. These include questions about the novelty of the work in light of existing literature, the appropriateness and rigor of the methodological approaches, the clarity and robustness of the reported results, and the strength and validity of the conclusions drawn from the findings.
R: We thank this reviewer for all positive comments and insightful comments/suggestions.
Comments:
Q1.1 Introduction - “First, existing studies focus mainly on discrete developmental stages (e.g., the third trimester 19 , neonatal period, adolescence, and adulthood), without provided a continuous spatiotemporal perspective from prenatal development through late adulthood.” This is not true and misleading in light of Ref 23.
R: We have rephrased the relevant descriptions and hopefully it is clearer now (page 4):
“First, most existing studies of the functional hierarchy have focused on discrete developmental stages (e.g., the third trimester 19, neonatal period 18, adolescence 20,21 and adulthood 3,22), resulting in a fragmented perspective that obscures fine-grained transitions and nonlinear dynamics of cortical gradients across the full age continuum. Moreover, prior work has often been limited by small (e.g., N < 100) 18,19 or modest (N = hundreds to thousands) 16,20–22 sample sizes, along with a predominant reliance on linear modelling to characterize gradient development 19,20,22. Although a recent study 23 established a continuous, nonlinear mapping of functional gradients from birth to 100 years of age, the inferred developmental patterns remain constrained by a modest sample size (N = 3,556) and particularly sparse data coverage during childhood.”
Q1.2 Introduction - “Furthermore, methodological limitations, such as small (less than one hundred) or modest (hundreds to thousands) sample sizes and an overreliance on simplistic linear modelling approaches, fundamentally constrain our ability to capture nonlinear neurodevelopmental dynamics.” This is also not true. The methods used for data processing and analysis (FreeSurfer, GAMLSS, etc.) in the current work are mostly publicly available and are quite standard. There are no methodological hurdles preventing other groups from carrying out similar work.
R: We would like to clarify this point raised by this reviewer. We agree that both standard preprocessing pipelines (e.g., FreeSurfer) and advanced nonlinear modeling frameworks (e.g., GAMLSS) are well-established within the community. Our aim was not to imply that these tools are non-standard, but to highlight that many prior studies have yet to fully integrate large-scale datasets with nonlinear modeling to characterize developmental trajectories in the cortical hierarchy. We have revised the sentence accordingly (page 4):
“First, most existing studies of the functional hierarchy have focused on discrete developmental stages (e.g., the third trimester 19, neonatal period 18, adolescence 20,21 and adulthood 3,22), resulting in a 1 fragmented perspective that obscures fine-grained transitions and nonlinear dynamics of cortical gradients across the full age continuum. Moreover, prior work has often been limited by small (e.g., N < 100) 18,19 or modest (N = hundreds to thousands) 16,20–22 sample sizes, along with a predominant reliance on linear modelling to characterize gradient development 19,20,22.”
Q1.3 Introduction - “Second, current conceptual frameworks predominantly emphasize functional gradient remodelling during development while largely overlooking its structural foundations. In mature brains, the S-A axis aligns spatially with structural features indexed by cortical thickness, intracortical myelination, and intrinsic geometry.” This is not true. Association between primary gradients and structural gradients has already been investigated for example in reference 23.
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. We have revised the text to clarify this (page 4-5):
“Second, current research frameworks lack the capacity to delineate how functional hierarchies coevolve with specific structural features, such as cortical thickness 2,6,24, intracortical myelination 2,8,9, and intrinsic geometry 3,25, across the lifespan. While the S-A axis aligns spatially with these structural attributes in mature brains, the developmental synchrony between functional and structural maturation remains largely unclear, particularly given their distinct maturational timelines in early life 2. A previous study 23 reported coupling between lifespan changes in functional gradients and a composite structural gradient derived from multiple features; however, its analysis strategy that integrates multiple structural properties prior to dimensionality reduction does not directly assess the contribution of specific structural properties to the emergence of functional gradients.”
Q1.4 Why 26 age groups? This creates artificial temporal demarcations between different life periods that do not necessarily reflect true biological development. This is particularly problematic when different brain regions have distinct development timelines that do not coincide with these artificial temporal partitions. It is uncertain if age grouping will result in artificial disconunity in the analysis, not just at the global whole-brain level but also local vertex level.
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. Currently, there is no universally accepted standard for defining age groups. Our selection of 26 age groups was informed by developmental principles indicating that brain maturation occurs rapidly during infancy and childhood but slows progressively through adolescence and adulthood. Therefore, we applied finer age partitions at younger stages and broader intervals at later ages to better capture these nonlinear developmental dynamics.
To further address the concern regarding potential artificial discontinuities, we also conducted complementary analyses at the individual level without imposing predefined age bins. Specifically, functional gradients were computed for each participant and then clustered across all individuals, using chronological age as a quasi-continuous variable. This individual-level approach confirmed the main findings of three phases of functional gradient development: (Phase I) early anterior-posterior differentiation during infancy, (Phase II) emergence of the S-A gradient in early childhood, and (Phase III) its gradual expansion, refinement, and stabilization throughout adolescence and adulthood. The convergence between the group-based and individual-level analyses indicate that our conclusions are not affected by the chosen age-grouping scheme.
The Supplementary analyses were added in the revised manuscript (page 7):
Results: “The three developmental phases were also identified through both individual-level gradient clustering without predefined age bins and within-age-group-harmonized analysis (Supplementary Fig. 3, 4). This indicates that the observed patterns were robust and not driven by specific age-grouping schemes or site related confounds.”
Supplementary Results: “To validate the robustness of our findings, we first verified that developmental phases identified in the group-based analyses were consistently reproduced in individual-level clustering without predefined age bins, confirming that the observed patterns were not driven by the specific age-grouping scheme (Supplementary Fig. 3).”
Supplementary Fig. 3 | Distinct growth stages of the sensorimotor-association gradient across the lifespan identified from individual gradients. a, K-means clustering analysis based on the pairwise correlations between the individual gradient maps, resulting in three clusters. b, Three distinct phases of the S-A gradient are visualized via multidimensional scaling (MDS). “Dimension 1” and “dimension 2” are defined as the first and second axes obtained through MDS of the functional distance matrix.
Q1.5 How does the choice of 26 age groups influence the clustering results? The patterns shown in Figure 1b may vary not only with the number of age groups but also with how these groups are distributed over time. Moreover, the age grouping adopted from the authors’ previous publication may not be appropriate here, as this study focuses on gradients rather than simple features of functional connectivity. The authors should demonstrate that this age grouping does not introduce bias by comparing it against clustering results obtained from the entire dataset without imposing predefined age groups.
R: To evaluate whether the clustering results were influenced by the choice of age-group definitions, we conducted an additional analysis at the individual level across all participants without imposing any predefined age bins. Functional gradients were derived separately for each participant, and clustering was then performed on the complete dataset using chronological age as a continuous variable.
This individual-level analysis reproduced the same three major developmental phases identified in the age-binned analysis: (Phase I) early anterior-posterior differentiation during infancy, (Phase II) emergence of the sensorimotor-association (S-A) gradient in early childhood, and (Phase III) progressive expansion and stabilization of this gradient through adolescence and adulthood. The high consistency between the group-based and individual-level results demonstrates that the choice of 26 age groups does not bias the clustering outcomes. These findings confirm the robustness of our developmental trajectory characterization and validate that the observed patterns are not artifacts of grouping strategy.
Q1.6 How is the difference in sample size across age groups dealt with? The authors did a “balanced resampling analysis” by equal resampling across age bins. However, it is unclear why the 16 “age bins” are different from the 26 “age groups”. Also, does the fact that resampling uniformly with a smaller number of samples per age bin still replicates the main results suggest that the large sample size used in the study may not be necessary?
R: We complemented the age-binned analysis with individual-level clustering that does not depend on predefined bins. This analysis again confirmed the same three developmental phases, demonstrating that the main findings are robust to differences in group size and binning scheme.
The use of 16 “age bins” in the balanced resampling analysis reflects a methodological adjustment aimed at ensuring an adequate and comparable number of participants in each bin for statistical resampling, rather than a conceptual change from the 26 developmental age groups used in the main analysis.
Regarding the necessity of a large sample size, as detailed in our response to Q1.8, larger samples substantially improve the stability and reliability of lifespan growth curve estimates, particularly at the regional and vertex levels, by reducing variance and enhancing the precision of developmental trajectory characterization. Thus, while smaller, balanced subsamples supports the validity of our conclusion, the full sample remains essential for achieving optimal reliability and generalizability of brain gradient trajectories.
Q1.7 How are differences in data variances between datasets and across time dealt with?
There can be nonlinear variance changes across age groups and within age groups and also across the different datasets and within the datasets.
R: We took several steps to minimize potential biases introduced by variance differences across datasets and age groups in the original analyses.
First, at the preprocessing stage, all datasets were processed using identical pipelines: projection to fsaverage_LR32k, nuisance regression with 24 motion parameters plus WM, CSF, and global signal, linear detrending, temporal bandpass filtering (0.01-0.08 Hz), scrubbing (FD > 0.5 mm with one preceding and two subsequent volumes interpolated), surface smoothing (FWHM = 6 mm), and resampling to fsaverage4 space. These harmonized pipelines ensured comparable signal properties across datasets.
Second, at the modelling stage, we explicitly accounted for age- and site-related heteroscedasticity using the GAMLSS framework with a flexible skew exponential power type 4 (SEP4) distribution. Specifically, we modeled the variance (scale parameter, σ) as a smooth function of age and sex (sigma.fo=~bs(Age) + Sex), which accommodates nonlinear variance changes across the lifespan. Site was further included as a random effect to capture both mean and variance differences across datasets.
Third, model diagnostics confirmed the adequacy of our approach. We examined normalized quantile residuals, residuals-fitted plots, kernel density estimates, and normal Q-Q plots (Supplementary Fig. 28), all of which indicated well-behaved residuals without systematic trends. Detrended Owen’s plots further showed that residuals remained within nonparametric confidence intervals (Supplementary Fig. 29). Together, these diagnostics suggest that the GAMLSS effectively captured heteroscedasticity.
Finally, sensitivity analyses using a leave-one-site-out strategy demonstrated that our main findings were highly consistent across datasets, supporting the robustness of our results against potential variance differences.
Q1.8 A large sample size like the one used in this paper is not always accessible to all researchers. Please show empirical evidence that such a large sample size gives conclusions that cannot be drawn using a smaller sample size.
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. To empirically evaluate the benefits of large sample sizes, we performed a resampling-based analysis while controlling for both age and sex distributions. Specifically, the lifespan range (32 PMW to 80 years) was divided into 10 equal intervals, and subsamples were drawn while preserving the original proportions of age and sex within each interval. For global- and system-level analyses, sample sizes were varied from 200 to 33,000 participants, with finer increments at smaller sizes. For regional-level analyses, 13 predefined sampling conditions were used. For each sample size, we performed 50 independent resampling iterations, refitted the lifespan growth curves, and computed the mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) relative to the reference curve estimated from the full dataset. The minimum sample size was defined as the point at which the observed MAE/RMSE decreased to within 1.5 times the error estimated at the maximum sample size for regional-level gradient values.
The results showed that both MAE and RMSE decreased as sample size increased. At the global and system levels, error dropped sharply when sample size grew from a few hundred to ~5,000 participants, after which gains plateaued. At the regional level, required sample sizes varied across cortical vertices. A sample size of at least ~6,000 participants was needed for more than 50% of cortical vertices to achieve stable error levels, while ~25% of vertices required even larger samples.
In sum, these analyses demonstrate that larger sample sizes substantially enhance the stability and reliability of lifespan growth curve estimates, particularly at the regional scale. These results provide empirical guidance on the minimum sample sizes required for robust conclusions in future lifespan neuroimaging studies. We have added relevant results in the revised manuscript (page 16):
“To evaluate the influence of sample size on our findings, we conducted a resampling-based sensitivity analysis, varying sample sizes from 200 to 33,000 participants. We observed that both mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) decreased with increasing sample size (Supplementary Fig. 17). Notably, errors at the global and system levels dropped sharply until about 5,000 participants, after which gains plateaued. Furthermore, at the regional level, a sample size of ~6,000 participants is necessary to achieve stable error estimates for more than half of the cortical vertices, while a quarter of vertices required even larger samples. This work confirms that larger samples are crucial for reliable gradient growth curves, especially at the regional scale, and provide valuable guidance for future lifespan neuroimaging studies.”
Supplementary Fig. 17 | Relationship between sample size and fitting error for gradient measures. a, Relationship between sample size and fitting error for global-level gradient measures (MAE shown in blue, RMSE in red). b, Relationship between sample size and fitting error for system-level gradient measures (MAE in the left panel, RMSE in the right panel). c, Relationship between sample size and fitting error for regional-level gradient values. The minimum sample size at which the MAE (left) /RMSE (right) reached a stable plateau for each vertex is mapped onto the cortical surface. 5 The pie charts summarize the distribution of these minimum sample size across all vertices. Sample sizes ranged from 200 to 33,000 participants, with 50 resampling iterations per size, and age/sex distributions were preserved across 10 lifespan intervals (32 PMW to 80 years).
Q1.9 Anterior-posterior gradient during early infancy – This is contradictory to previous observation that the SA gradient already exists at birth. The SA gradient does not start to occur at 3 months but before that.
R: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment and the opportunity to clarify. In our data, we observed a prominent anterior-posterior (A-P) gradient during the prenatal and neonatal periods, which progressively transitions into a more differentiated S-A gradient after approximately 3 months of age. This observation of an A-P gradient in early infancy is consistent with prior studies. For instance, Xia et al. (2024) reported the emergence of an anterior-posterior gradient as early as 34.6 postmenstrual weeks 1. Lariviere et al. (2020) described anterior-posterior variations in term-born neonates, interpreting these as an immature precursor of the differentiation between unimodal and transmodal areas 2.
The apparent inconsistency with Ref23 likely reflects methodological differences. Specifically, Ref23 employed a generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) to fit gradient development across the entire age range. Given the brevity of the early developmental window and the relatively small sample size available, such modeling may smooth or shape the less differentiated early-stage patterns into a more continuous S-A trajectory. In contrast, our approach used group-level analyses within discrete age bins, enabling us to directly characterize gradient architecture at each developmental stage without imposing model-based continuity across age. We have revised the text by adding a small discussion (page 18):
“Notably, we found that the functional topography at birth is not characterized by the S-A gradient but is instead dominated by an anterior-posterior differentiation. This finding is aligned with previous studies of preterm, term-born, and neonatal cohorts 18,19, suggesting that this pattern represents a developmental precursor to the mature S-A gradient. In contrast, one recent study 23 suggests that the S-A gradient is already present at birth. The discrepancy may partly arise from methodological differences: the previous study 23 applied lifespan generalized additive mixed modeling, which could smooth over less differentiated early-stage patterns. Our stage-specific analyses, by comparison, capture gradient organization directly at each period, offering a more fine-grained characterization of early functional topography.”
Q1.10 Grouping the broad age range from 5 years to 80 years as a single phase (Phase III) is too coarse and does not reflect the fact that growth inflection points happen quite often during adolescence.
R: We would like to further clarify this point. Our analysis for defining Phase III was not to suggest that age span from 5 to 80 years constitutes a homogenous developmental stage. Rather, Phase III was conceptualized as a broader period of gradient stabilization and refinement-a stage in which the S-A gradient, once established, undergoes progressive fine-tuned throughout childhood, adolescence, and adulthood, and then continues to evolve into late life. We have clarified this point in the revised manuscript (page 19):
“our definition of Phase III (5-80 years) reflects the prolonged refinement and stabilization of the S-A gradient from childhood, adolescence to adulthood, rather than developmental uniformity through this period.”
Q1.11 Datasets like the developing HCP (dHCP) use gestational age. Postnatal datasets such as the BCP use chronological age. How is the discrepancy between gestational age and chronological age resolved?
R: To ensure consistency across datasets, we converted gestational age in the dHCP dataset into chronological age by treating 40 gestational weeks as the time of birth (i.e., 0 years). Chronological age was then calculated as:
(𝐺𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑎𝑙 𝑎𝑔𝑒 𝑎𝑡 𝑠𝑐𝑎𝑛−40)×7
𝐶ℎ𝑟𝑜𝑛𝑜𝑙𝑜𝑔𝑖𝑐𝑎𝑙 𝑎𝑔𝑒 (𝑦𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑠)=
“To align the dHCP dataset with other cohorts, we converted gestational age to chronological age. The conversion was based on the assumption that 40 gestational weeks corresponds to birth (0 years of chronological age). The specific formula applied was: Chronological age (years) = (Gestational age at scan – 40) × 7 / 365. This procedure ensured all ages were referenced to a consistent postnatal timeline.”
Q1.12 “Collectively, these results revealed previously unreported spatiotemporal patterns and critical neurodevelopmental milestones of the functional hierarchy, as characterized by the initiation, establishment, and expansion/stability of the S-A axis of cortical functional organization.” Again, this is untrue in light of ref 23.
R: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. The related statements have been removed from the revised version.
Q1.13 Range and variance are measuring almost the same thing, i.e., the spread of the gradient values, and are therefore redundant. Please pick one to report.
R: While both range and standard deviation quantify aspects of distribution spread, they emphasize distinct properties. The range captures the full extent of gradient differentiation (maximum-minimum), highlighting the span of the axis and sensitivity to extreme values. In contrast, the standard deviation reflects the average dispersion of all gradient values (not just the maximum and minimum) around the mean, providing a more robust, outlier-resistant measure of variability. For example, consider two groups of numbers with the same range: one group is tightly clustered around the mean, and the other is spread out more evenly between the minimum and maximum values. Both groups have the same range, but the first group will have a smaller standard deviation, indicating less variability around the mean, whereas the second group will have a larger standard deviation, reflecting greater dispersion. Because these two indices offer complementary perspectives‒one emphasizing the maximal differentiation and the other overall dispersion‒we report both to provide a fuller characterization of developmental and topographical features of the gradient.
Q1.14 In Figure 2c and throughout the paper, it is unclear what “gradient score” is referring to.
R: To improve clarity, we have revised the terminology throughout the manuscript and figure legends, replacing “gradient score” with “gradient value”. This change more accurately reflects the numerical values derived from the gradient decomposition.
Q1.15 The results shown in Figure 2e seem to indicate that the SA gradient changes very little after 20 years. This contradicts Figs 2a and 2b and other results shown in the paper.
R: We would like to make a clarification about this point. First, the apparent stability of the S-A gradient after age 20 in Fig. 2e was partly due to the original colormap design rather than the underlying results. Specifically, the broad white center of the colormap compressed the visual contrast around zero values, making age-related changes less discernible. In the revised figure (see updated Fig. 2e), we applied a colormap with more balanced contrast to better capture subtle variations across adulthood.
Second, our analyses do indicate that the S-A gradient continues to change after early adulthood, although at a slower rate compared with the rapid alterations observed in early childhood. These adult changes are consistent with the global- and system-level results shown in Fig 2a and 2b, which demonstrate relative stabilization of gradient measures from the third decade onward to early aging, while still exhibiting gradual refinements at the regional levels.
Fig. 2 | Lifespan growth of the sensorimotor-association gradient. a, Lifespan growth curves (top panel) and growth rate curves (bottom panel) for global gradient measures. The solid line represents the 50th centile (median), while the dotted lines represent the 5th, 25th, 75th, and 95th centiles. The growth rate was estimated by the first derivative of the median growth curve, with a 95% confidence interval (shaded in gray) obtained from 1,000 bootstrap resamplings. The horizontal dotted line (y=0) marks the transition from growth to decline, with the peak age indicated by a purple dot. b, Lifespan growth curves of gradient range and standard deviation for each functional system defined according to the age-specific Yeo 7-network atlas 30,34,35. c, Lifespan growth of the gradient value for each functional system. The peak age is marked by a black dot. d, Contributions to lifespan growth of the S-A gradient from each functional system, estimated via knockout-based simulation analysis (left panel). A repeated-measures ANOVA tested variations in system contributions across developmental phases (right panel). ***, p<0.001. e, Lifespan growth rate maps of the S-A gradient at representative ages. f, Lifespan growth axis of the S-A gradient. The left panel shows regional gradient values across age. PCA identified the first component as the dominant lifespan growth axis, explaining 65.4% of the variance (middle panel). The growth axis was divided into 20 decile bins, and mean gradient values were computed for all vertices within each bin (right panel). g, Spatial correlation between the lifespan growth axis and the evolutionary hierarchy. Evolutionary hierarchy was quantified using macaque-to-human cortical expansion 32. Statistical significance was assessed via 1,000 non-parametric spin permutation tests 36. CI, confidence interval; VIS, visual; SM, somatomotor; DA, dorsal attention; VA, ventral attention; LIM, limbic; FP, frontoparietal; DM, default-mode; w, week; m, month; yr, year.
Q1.16 T1-weighted and T2-weighted images are not quantitative and can have arbitrary signal gains associated with different scanners, sequences, and choices of acquisition parameters. It is unclear how this is dealt with in this study, which involves datasets from quite a number of different sources.
R: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. It is indeed true that T1-weighted and T2-weighted images are not inherently quantitative, and their signal intensities can vary across scanners, sequences, and acquisition protocols.
Nevertheless, the T1w/T2w ratio provides a reliable proxy for relative cortical myelin content because myelin consistently shortens T1 relaxation times (increasing T1w signal) and T2 relaxation times (decreasing T2w signal), producing a systematic contrast that is amplified when taking their ratio 6,7. This approach has been widely adopted in developmental, clinical and comparative studies 6,8–11. Importantly, several studies have demonstrated that the T1w/T2w ratio produces robust and anatomically meaningful spatial patterns that remain consistent across different scanners and acquisition settings. For example, Glasser et al. reported that group-average datasets acquired on different scanners with different sequences at independent sites yielded qualitatively very similar results 6,7.
In the present study, we took several steps to further mitigate site-related variability. First, during preprocessing we applied biases and intensity normalization, which reduce transmit field biases and minimize intensity inhomogeneities. These steps are critical for improving cross-site comparability of T1w/T2w-derived myelin maps. Second, in our statistical modeling, we explicitly included site as a random effect in the GAMLSS framework, thereby adjusting for potential residual site-specific differences when estimating growth trajectories.
Together, these strategies substantially reduce concerns regarding inter-scanner variability and support the robustness of our T1w/T2w-based myelin estimates across multiple datasets. In the revised manuscript, we have added relevant description and hopefully it is clearer now (page 29).
“To mitigate inter-scanner variability and enhance cross-site comparability, all T1w and T2w images underwent bias correction and intensity normalization prior to the computation of the T1w/T2w ratio.……. we fitted the growth curves of the structural attributes for each vertex via GAMLSS with age and sex as fixed effects, and site as a random effect.”
Q1.17 Were the inter-vertex geometric distances normalized with respect to the “total” inter-vertex distance. Since the brain is changing in size across the lifespan, it is unclear how the brain size will affect the analysis on geometric distance.
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. To account for inter-individual differences in brain size and their potential impact on geodesic distance measures, we normalized geodesic distances by the square root of the cortical surface area. This was done when analyzing distances between vertices within the top and bottom 5% of S-A gradient values. We then re-fitted the lifespan growth curves using these normalized distances, and the results remained highly consistent with our original findings. We have rephrased the relevant sections in Methods and Results as follows:
Methods (page 28): “To account for inter-individual differences in brain size, geodesic distances were normalized by the square root of the cortical surface area.”
Results (page 12): “For each individual, we calculated the mean normalized geometric distances between paired vertices with extreme gradient values. This geometric distance exhibited a nonlinear trajectory across the lifespan, peaking during young adulthood (20.7 years, 95% bootstrap CI: 17.2–23.2), followed by a gradual decline (Fig. 4b).”
Q1.18 Why multi-step Procrustes alignment using age groups, instead of constructing the gradient template directly from the gradients of the individuals?
R: We adopted a multi-step Procrustes alignment based on age groups to reduce potential biases arising from sample size imbalances and age-related variations in gradient topography. If a group-level gradient template were constructed directly from all individual embeddings, the resulting template would likely be disproportionately influenced by age groups with larger sample size and might obscure meaningful developmental stage-specific differences. By first aligning gradients within narrower age groups and then iteratively converging toward a common template, our approach ensures that the reference template captures both shared organizational features and age-specific variations in gradient topography. This strategy provides a more balanced and representative framework for comparing gradients across the lifespan. We have rephrased the relevant sections (page 23):
“To ensure accurate comparisons between groups, we applied Procrustes rotation 79 to align age-specific group-level functional gradients to iterative group-level reference gradients……Compared with constructing the template directly from individual gradients, this multi-step alignment strategy reduces biases from sample size imbalances and development variations in gradient topography.”
Q1.19 Cortical surfaces were generated using different pipelines and hence cortical thickness measurements are not consistent. For example, iBEAT surfaces and FreeSurfer might not be entirely consistent. The conclusions might be affected by this inconsistency.
R: We used different cortical surface reconstruction pipelines for different age groups (iBEAT for infants and FreeSurfer for older participants). This decision was intentional 12–14, as each tool has been specifically optimized for the developmental stage it targets. Applying a single pipeline across the entire age range would likely introduce greater bias, since adult-oriented tools such as FreeSurfer are suboptimal for infant brains, while infant-tailored pipelines are not designed for adult anatomy.
Previous validation studies support the appropriateness of this strategy 12–14. For example, Wang et al. (2023) demonstrated that iBEAT V2.0, a deep learning-based pipeline optimized for infant cortical reconstruction, produces accurate and reproducible surfaces across scanners and imaging protocols 12. Similarly, Makropoulos et al. (2018) established a neonatal minimal processing pipeline designed to capture the unique anatomical features of early development 13. For older participants, the widely adopted Human Connectome Project pipeline and FreeSurfer have been rigorously validated in multisite settings and are considered standards for adult cortical surface analysis 14.
By using pipelines tailored to the anatomical characteristics of each age group, we aimed to minimize reconstruction errors and enhance the reliability of cortical thickness estimation across the lifespan. All subsequent analyses were conducted on surfaces registered to a common template space, further mitigating concerns about cross-pipeline inconsistency. We have rephrased the relevant sections in the Supplementary Methods section (page 2):
“This age-appropriate pipeline selection minimizes cortical reconstruction bias across the lifespan, and all surfaces were subsequently registered to a common template to ensure cross-pipeline comparability.”
Q1.20 The fMRI data is not necessarily scanned under the same condition, even in the lifespan HCP datasets. For example, the BCP data for the first three years are scanned with the children asleep. How is this discrepancy handled to ensure the validity of findings?
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. Indeed, scanning conditions necessarily vary across lifespan datasets due to practical and ethical considerations. For example, in the Baby Connectome Project (BCP), infants aged 0-35 months were typically scanned during natural sleep, whereas older children could be scanned either awake or asleep depending on feasibility 15. Similarly, in the Developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP), virtually all infants were scanned during natural sleep. In contrast, large-scale adolescent and adult cohorts such as ABCD, HCP, ADNI, CamCAN, and UK Biobank explicitly required participants to remain awake during resting-state scans (eyes open or eyes closed, depending on protocol). Unfortunately, precise per-scan records of sleep/awake state are not publicly available for dHCP and BCP, preventing direct stratification by brain state.
We fully acknowledge that brain state can influence functional activity patterns 16 and may affect gradient estimation. However, several factors mitigate this concern. First, the gradients observed show robust and biologically plausible age-related trajectories that are consistent across datasets and scales, suggesting that they are not solely driven by state differences. Second, all datasets underwent harmonized preprocessing pipelines, which help minimize systematic biases. Third, the vary large sample size provides statistical stability, reducing the influence of individual-level variation in scan conditions. We now explicitly note this as a limitation in the revised manuscript (page 21):
“Finally, the large fMRI datasets exhibited heterogeneity in scanning states: neonate and infant data were primarily acquired during natural sleep, whereas children and adults were scanned during wakefulness. Given differences in functional brain activity between sleep and wake states 73, we cannot rule out the potential influence of this acquisition discrepancy on the observed patterns. Future studies that control for this variable by using identical scanning states across age groups will be important to clarify this issue.”
Q1.21 Phase I ends at one month postnatally, and Phase III begins at age five. These timepoints coincide with the end of the dHCP and the end of the BCP, respectively. The dHCP, BCP, and the remaining lifespan HCP studies use different imaging protocols. Therefore, it is likely that the demarcation of Phases I, II, and III might be an artifact of differences in image acquisition.
R: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this point. To assess whether the phase boundaries coinciding with the transitions between the dHCP, BCP, and HCP datasets could be driven by differences in acquisition protocols, we explicitly evaluated the potential influence of such site and protocol effects. A single harmonization across the entire lifespan would not be appropriate in this context, as the topographic architecture of functional connectivity systematically changes with age. Applying one global harmonization procedure could inadvertently distort age-specific topographic features or impose artificial similarity across distinct developmental stages.
Instead, we minimized acquisition-related variability by removing site-specific effects within each age group before gradient estimation. Specifically, for each age group, site was modeled as a random effect in the vertex-wise FC data and regressed out prior to constructing group-level connectivity matrices and computing gradients. When gradients and clustering were derived from these within-age-group-harmonized data, the same three developmental phases (early anterior-posterior differentiation; emergence of the S-A axis in early childhood; and subsequent expansion, refinement, and stabilization) were reproduced and closely matched the results reported in the main text. Moreover, when determining optimal number of clusters, both 3- and 4-cluster solutions were identified with equal frequency across clustering indices. We reported the 3-cluster solution in the main text, while the 4-cluster solution only further subdivided the earliest phase (32w to 3 months). This concordance indicates that the observed phase boundaries reflect genuine developmental transitions rather than artifacts arising from dataset boundaries or acquisition differences. We have added a corresponding description in the revised Results (page 7) and Supplementary Results (page 3):
Results: “The three developmental phases were also identified through both individual-level gradient clustering without predefined age bins and within-age-group-harmonized analysis (Supplementary Fig. 3, 4). This indicates that the observed patterns were robust and not driven by specific age-grouping schemes or site related confounds.”
Supplementary Results: “To ensure that the phase boundaries were not artifacts of differences in acquisition protocols across datasets, site was modeled as random effect and regressed out within each age group prior to computing group-level connectivity matrices and gradients. Analyses using these harmonized data reproduced the same three phases, indicating that the observed phase boundaries reflect genuine developmental transitions rather than dataset or acquisition differences (Supplementary Fig. 4).”
Supplementary Fig. 4 | Distinct growth stages of the sensorimotor-association gradient across the lifespan from the harmonized functional connectome. a, S-A gradient maps generated for 26 distinct age groups derived from the harmonized functional connectome. b, K-means clustering analysis based on the pairwise correlations between the 26 group-based gradient maps, resulting in three clusters (main text) and an alternative four-cluster solution that further subdivides the earliest phase. c, Three distinct phases of the S-A gradient are visualized via multidimensional scaling (MDS). “Dimension 1” and “dimension 2” are defined as the first and second axes obtained through MDS of the functional distance matrix. d, Distribution of gradient values in the S-A axis across lifespan. w, week; m, month; yr, year.
Q1.22 How is longitudinal information, repeated observations of each subject, dealt with? Not doing so might bias the results.
R: To minimize potential bias introduced by repeated measurements from the same participants, we restricted our analyses to a single imaging session per individual across all longitudinal datasets. This ensure that each participant contributed only once to the cross-sectional lifespan analyses, thereby preventing inflated sample sizes or undue weighting of individuals with repeated scans. This procedure is described in the Methods section of the revised manuscript (page 22):
“For participants with multiple imaging sessions, only the first scan was selected for inclusion, ensuring that each individual contributed a single observation to the analyses.”
Q1.23 The effects of sex may vary nonlinearly across age, especially given the long developmental time span covered in this study. However, this nonlinearity does not appear to have been modeled.
R: To test whether the effects of sex on gradient measures vary nonlinearly across the lifespan, in the revised manuscript we performed additional analyses at the global, system, and regional levels.
Specifically, we used the GAMLSS framework, which flexibly captures nonlinear trajectories across age. Two nested models were compared: a baseline model including main effects of age and sex, and a full model including an age-by-sex interaction term. Both models controlled for mean FD as a covariate, and site was modeled as a random effect. Significance of the interaction was assessed using the generalized likelihood ratio tests (GLRT), with FDR correction applied (q < 0.05).
At the global level, females showed significantly higher explanation ratio, gradient range, and variation compared with males across the lifespan (all p<0.05, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 35a). At the system level, the overall hierarchical organization was preserved, with the default-mode and frontoparietal systems consistently showed higher gradient ranges and standard deviations, while the sensorimotor system displayed lower values throughout life. Importantly, females exhibited significantly greater gradient ranges and variations than males (all p<0.001, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 35b). Moreover, peak age analyses revealed that in several functional systems, including visual, limbic, frontoparietal, and default mode networks, females demonstrated significantly later maturational peaks than males (all p<0.001, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 35c & Supplementary Table 8), suggesting delayed maturational timing in females. At the regional level, females exhibited higher gradient values in temporal, precuneus, medial prefrontal and somatomotor regions, whereas males showed higher values in occipital and lateral prefrontal regions (p<0.001, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 35d).
These findings have been incorporated into the Supplementary Methods (page 3) and Results sections (page 7):
Supplementary Methods:
“To test whether the effects of sex on gradient measures vary nonlinearly across the lifespan, we performed additional analyses at the global, system, and regional levels. Specifically, we used the GAMLSS framework, which flexibly captures nonlinear trajectories across age. Two nested models were compared: a baseline model including main effects of age and sex, and a full model including an age-by-sex interaction term. Both models, controlled for mean FD as a covariate, and site was modeled as a random effect. Significance of the interaction was assessed by comparing the model fits of the baseline and full models using the generalized likelihood ratio test (GLRT). All p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons using the FDR (q < 0.05). The direction of sex differences was determined based on the mean differences between the fitted sex-specific growth curves.”
