Q1.16 T1-weighted and T2-weighted images are not quantitative and can have arbitrary signal gains associated with different scanners, sequences, and choices of acquisition parameters. It is unclear how this is dealt with in this study, which involves datasets from quite a number of different sources.
R: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. It is indeed true that T1-weighted and T2-weighted images are not inherently quantitative, and their signal intensities can vary across scanners, sequences, and acquisition protocols.
Nevertheless, the T1w/T2w ratio provides a reliable proxy for relative cortical myelin content because myelin consistently shortens T1 relaxation times (increasing T1w signal) and T2 relaxation times (decreasing T2w signal), producing a systematic contrast that is amplified when taking their ratio 6,7. This approach has been widely adopted in developmental, clinical and comparative studies 6,8–11. Importantly, several studies have demonstrated that the T1w/T2w ratio produces robust and anatomically meaningful spatial patterns that remain consistent across different scanners and acquisition settings. For example, Glasser et al. reported that group-average datasets acquired on different scanners with different sequences at independent sites yielded qualitatively very similar results 6,7.
In the present study, we took several steps to further mitigate site-related variability. First, during preprocessing we applied biases and intensity normalization, which reduce transmit field biases and minimize intensity inhomogeneities. These steps are critical for improving cross-site comparability of T1w/T2w-derived myelin maps. Second, in our statistical modeling, we explicitly included site as a random effect in the GAMLSS framework, thereby adjusting for potential residual site-specific differences when estimating growth trajectories.
Together, these strategies substantially reduce concerns regarding inter-scanner variability and support the robustness of our T1w/T2w-based myelin estimates across multiple datasets. In the revised manuscript, we have added relevant description and hopefully it is clearer now (page 29).
“To mitigate inter-scanner variability and enhance cross-site comparability, all T1w and T2w images underwent bias correction and intensity normalization prior to the computation of the T1w/T2w ratio.……. we fitted the growth curves of the structural attributes for each vertex via GAMLSS with age and sex as fixed effects, and site as a random effect.”
Q1.17 Were the inter-vertex geometric distances normalized with respect to the “total” inter-vertex distance. Since the brain is changing in size across the lifespan, it is unclear how the brain size will affect the analysis on geometric distance.
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. To account for inter-individual differences in brain size and their potential impact on geodesic distance measures, we normalized geodesic distances by the square root of the cortical surface area. This was done when analyzing distances between vertices within the top and bottom 5% of S-A gradient values. We then re-fitted the lifespan growth curves using these normalized distances, and the results remained highly consistent with our original findings. We have rephrased the relevant sections in Methods and Results as follows:
Methods (page 28): “To account for inter-individual differences in brain size, geodesic distances were normalized by the square root of the cortical surface area.”
Results (page 12): “For each individual, we calculated the mean normalized geometric distances between paired vertices with extreme gradient values. This geometric distance exhibited a nonlinear trajectory across the lifespan, peaking during young adulthood (20.7 years, 95% bootstrap CI: 17.2–23.2), followed by a gradual decline (Fig. 4b).”
Q1.18 Why multi-step Procrustes alignment using age groups, instead of constructing the gradient template directly from the gradients of the individuals?
R: We adopted a multi-step Procrustes alignment based on age groups to reduce potential biases arising from sample size imbalances and age-related variations in gradient topography. If a group-level gradient template were constructed directly from all individual embeddings, the resulting template would likely be disproportionately influenced by age groups with larger sample size and might obscure meaningful developmental stage-specific differences. By first aligning gradients within narrower age groups and then iteratively converging toward a common template, our approach ensures that the reference template captures both shared organizational features and age-specific variations in gradient topography. This strategy provides a more balanced and representative framework for comparing gradients across the lifespan. We have rephrased the relevant sections (page 23):
“To ensure accurate comparisons between groups, we applied Procrustes rotation 79 to align age-specific group-level functional gradients to iterative group-level reference gradients……Compared with constructing the template directly from individual gradients, this multi-step alignment strategy reduces biases from sample size imbalances and development variations in gradient topography.”
Q1.19 Cortical surfaces were generated using different pipelines and hence cortical thickness measurements are not consistent. For example, iBEAT surfaces and FreeSurfer might not be entirely consistent. The conclusions might be affected by this inconsistency.
R: We used different cortical surface reconstruction pipelines for different age groups (iBEAT for infants and FreeSurfer for older participants). This decision was intentional 12–14, as each tool has been specifically optimized for the developmental stage it targets. Applying a single pipeline across the entire age range would likely introduce greater bias, since adult-oriented tools such as FreeSurfer are suboptimal for infant brains, while infant-tailored pipelines are not designed for adult anatomy.
Previous validation studies support the appropriateness of this strategy 12–14. For example, Wang et al. (2023) demonstrated that iBEAT V2.0, a deep learning-based pipeline optimized for infant cortical reconstruction, produces accurate and reproducible surfaces across scanners and imaging protocols 12. Similarly, Makropoulos et al. (2018) established a neonatal minimal processing pipeline designed to capture the unique anatomical features of early development 13. For older participants, the widely adopted Human Connectome Project pipeline and FreeSurfer have been rigorously validated in multisite settings and are considered standards for adult cortical surface analysis 14.
By using pipelines tailored to the anatomical characteristics of each age group, we aimed to minimize reconstruction errors and enhance the reliability of cortical thickness estimation across the lifespan. All subsequent analyses were conducted on surfaces registered to a common template space, further mitigating concerns about cross-pipeline inconsistency. We have rephrased the relevant sections in the Supplementary Methods section (page 2):
“This age-appropriate pipeline selection minimizes cortical reconstruction bias across the lifespan, and all surfaces were subsequently registered to a common template to ensure cross-pipeline comparability.”
Q1.20 The fMRI data is not necessarily scanned under the same condition, even in the lifespan HCP datasets. For example, the BCP data for the first three years are scanned with the children asleep. How is this discrepancy handled to ensure the validity of findings?
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. Indeed, scanning conditions necessarily vary across lifespan datasets due to practical and ethical considerations. For example, in the Baby Connectome Project (BCP), infants aged 0-35 months were typically scanned during natural sleep, whereas older children could be scanned either awake or asleep depending on feasibility 15. Similarly, in the Developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP), virtually all infants were scanned during natural sleep. In contrast, large-scale adolescent and adult cohorts such as ABCD, HCP, ADNI, CamCAN, and UK Biobank explicitly required participants to remain awake during resting-state scans (eyes open or eyes closed, depending on protocol). Unfortunately, precise per-scan records of sleep/awake state are not publicly available for dHCP and BCP, preventing direct stratification by brain state.
We fully acknowledge that brain state can influence functional activity patterns 16 and may affect gradient estimation. However, several factors mitigate this concern. First, the gradients observed show robust and biologically plausible age-related trajectories that are consistent across datasets and scales, suggesting that they are not solely driven by state differences. Second, all datasets underwent harmonized preprocessing pipelines, which help minimize systematic biases. Third, the vary large sample size provides statistical stability, reducing the influence of individual-level variation in scan conditions. We now explicitly note this as a limitation in the revised manuscript (page 21):
“Finally, the large fMRI datasets exhibited heterogeneity in scanning states: neonate and infant data were primarily acquired during natural sleep, whereas children and adults were scanned during wakefulness. Given differences in functional brain activity between sleep and wake states 73, we cannot rule out the potential influence of this acquisition discrepancy on the observed patterns. Future studies that control for this variable by using identical scanning states across age groups will be important to clarify this issue.”
Q1.21 Phase I ends at one month postnatally, and Phase III begins at age five. These timepoints coincide with the end of the dHCP and the end of the BCP, respectively. The dHCP, BCP, and the remaining lifespan HCP studies use different imaging protocols. Therefore, it is likely that the demarcation of Phases I, II, and III might be an artifact of differences in image acquisition.
R: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this point. To assess whether the phase boundaries coinciding with the transitions between the dHCP, BCP, and HCP datasets could be driven by differences in acquisition protocols, we explicitly evaluated the potential influence of such site and protocol effects. A single harmonization across the entire lifespan would not be appropriate in this context, as the topographic architecture of functional connectivity systematically changes with age. Applying one global harmonization procedure could inadvertently distort age-specific topographic features or impose artificial similarity across distinct developmental stages.
Instead, we minimized acquisition-related variability by removing site-specific effects within each age group before gradient estimation. Specifically, for each age group, site was modeled as a random effect in the vertex-wise FC data and regressed out prior to constructing group-level connectivity matrices and computing gradients. When gradients and clustering were derived from these within-age-group-harmonized data, the same three developmental phases (early anterior-posterior differentiation; emergence of the S-A axis in early childhood; and subsequent expansion, refinement, and stabilization) were reproduced and closely matched the results reported in the main text. Moreover, when determining optimal number of clusters, both 3- and 4-cluster solutions were identified with equal frequency across clustering indices. We reported the 3-cluster solution in the main text, while the 4-cluster solution only further subdivided the earliest phase (32w to 3 months). This concordance indicates that the observed phase boundaries reflect genuine developmental transitions rather than artifacts arising from dataset boundaries or acquisition differences. We have added a corresponding description in the revised Results (page 7) and Supplementary Results (page 3):
Results: “The three developmental phases were also identified through both individual-level gradient clustering without predefined age bins and within-age-group-harmonized analysis (Supplementary Fig. 3, 4). This indicates that the observed patterns were robust and not driven by specific age-grouping schemes or site related confounds.”
Supplementary Results: “To ensure that the phase boundaries were not artifacts of differences in acquisition protocols across datasets, site was modeled as random effect and regressed out within each age group prior to computing group-level connectivity matrices and gradients. Analyses using these harmonized data reproduced the same three phases, indicating that the observed phase boundaries reflect genuine developmental transitions rather than dataset or acquisition differences (Supplementary Fig. 4).”
Supplementary Fig. 4 | Distinct growth stages of the sensorimotor-association gradient across the lifespan from the harmonized functional connectome. a, S-A gradient maps generated for 26 distinct age groups derived from the harmonized functional connectome. b, K-means clustering analysis based on the pairwise correlations between the 26 group-based gradient maps, resulting in three clusters (main text) and an alternative four-cluster solution that further subdivides the earliest phase. c, Three distinct phases of the S-A gradient are visualized via multidimensional scaling (MDS). “Dimension 1” and “dimension 2” are defined as the first and second axes obtained through MDS of the functional distance matrix. d, Distribution of gradient values in the S-A axis across lifespan. w, week; m, month; yr, year.
Q1.22 How is longitudinal information, repeated observations of each subject, dealt with? Not doing so might bias the results.
R: To minimize potential bias introduced by repeated measurements from the same participants, we restricted our analyses to a single imaging session per individual across all longitudinal datasets. This ensure that each participant contributed only once to the cross-sectional lifespan analyses, thereby preventing inflated sample sizes or undue weighting of individuals with repeated scans. This procedure is described in the Methods section of the revised manuscript (page 22):
“For participants with multiple imaging sessions, only the first scan was selected for inclusion, ensuring that each individual contributed a single observation to the analyses.”
Q1.23 The effects of sex may vary nonlinearly across age, especially given the long developmental time span covered in this study. However, this nonlinearity does not appear to have been modeled.
R: To test whether the effects of sex on gradient measures vary nonlinearly across the lifespan, in the revised manuscript we performed additional analyses at the global, system, and regional levels.
Specifically, we used the GAMLSS framework, which flexibly captures nonlinear trajectories across age. Two nested models were compared: a baseline model including main effects of age and sex, and a full model including an age-by-sex interaction term. Both models controlled for mean FD as a covariate, and site was modeled as a random effect. Significance of the interaction was assessed using the generalized likelihood ratio tests (GLRT), with FDR correction applied (q < 0.05).
At the global level, females showed significantly higher explanation ratio, gradient range, and variation compared with males across the lifespan (all p<0.05, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 35a). At the system level, the overall hierarchical organization was preserved, with the default-mode and frontoparietal systems consistently showed higher gradient ranges and standard deviations, while the sensorimotor system displayed lower values throughout life. Importantly, females exhibited significantly greater gradient ranges and variations than males (all p<0.001, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 35b). Moreover, peak age analyses revealed that in several functional systems, including visual, limbic, frontoparietal, and default mode networks, females demonstrated significantly later maturational peaks than males (all p<0.001, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 35c & Supplementary Table 8), suggesting delayed maturational timing in females. At the regional level, females exhibited higher gradient values in temporal, precuneus, medial prefrontal and somatomotor regions, whereas males showed higher values in occipital and lateral prefrontal regions (p<0.001, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 35d).
These findings have been incorporated into the Supplementary Methods (page 3) and Results sections (page 7):
Supplementary Methods:
“To test whether the effects of sex on gradient measures vary nonlinearly across the lifespan, we performed additional analyses at the global, system, and regional levels. Specifically, we used the GAMLSS framework, which flexibly captures nonlinear trajectories across age. Two nested models were compared: a baseline model including main effects of age and sex, and a full model including an age-by-sex interaction term. Both models, controlled for mean FD as a covariate, and site was modeled as a random effect. Significance of the interaction was assessed by comparing the model fits of the baseline and full models using the generalized likelihood ratio test (GLRT). All p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons using the FDR (q < 0.05). The direction of sex differences was determined based on the mean differences between the fitted sex-specific growth curves.”
Supplementary Results:
“To investigate whether sex differences in cortical gradient measures vary across age
reviewer_updating.target:
### Reviewer 1

General comments:
- Upon inspecting the code for the group-level gradient analysis, “Gradient_Analysis.m” in the publicly available repo, there are a few things that seem worth flagging for clarification. First, I see a potential flaw with the way that age-specific group-FC is computed: they apply Gaussian age weight within each bin (good), but then appear to average by the number of subjects rather than by the sum of the weights. That effectively makes the scale of the group FC depend on the age dispersion and sample size in each bin, and it means subjects contribute very unevenly within a bin in a way that isn’t clearly justified. Second, the use of a single reference age to anchor the alignment, followed by reordering the gradients back into chronological age, assumes that component identities and eigenvalue ordering are stable across the lifespan, something that has been measured elsewhere to not hold.
- In figure S3, which shows the clustering into lifespan stages based on individual gradients, the clusters in the MDS plot do not really look like clearly defined clusters but instead it looks like there are arbitrarily oriented cluster divisions. This is more suggestive of a “gradual transitions” narrative rather than a “distinct growth phases” narrative.
Further concerns are outlined below, using numbering consistent with the previous iteration.
Response 1.1: The current study however does not provide a “continuous” mapping of functional gradients because the temporal information is divided in the 26 clusters.
Response 1.3: It is unclear what is meant by “ its analysis strategy that integrates multiple structural properties prior to dimensionality reduction”. Gradients is a dimensionality reduction technique.
Response 1.4: If the results do not depend on binning, why is binning needed in the first place. The developmental phases are a somewhat artificial demarcation of the temporal developmental patterns since regional developmental patterns might not conform to these phases.
Response 1.5: Again, phases are very coarse groupings. Regional results might change with the age binning pattern.
Response 1.6: Although it is in general true that a larger sample size improves stability and reliability (provided that harmonization can be confirmed to be done correctly), it is unclear here what new neuroscientific findings exactly can be found here compared with studies of smaller sample sizes.
Response 1.7: The data, other than the fMRI data, was not processed using identical pipelines. There are additional acquisition and study design related variability that cannot be taken care of by using identical pipelines.
Response 1.9: The authors attribute the discrepancy with Ref 23 to methodological differences, suggesting that generalized additive mixed modeling (GAMM) 'smoothed over' early-stage patterns. However, a more parsimonious explanation lies in the dimensionality and rank-ordering of the eigenvectors.
It is well-documented that in the neonatal brain, the eigengap between the first and second gradients is often narrow, and the variance explained by the VS axis and the SA axis can be comparable. The 'emergence' of the S-A gradient at 3 months may simply represent a rank-swap between AP and SA gradients. Without showing both the first and second gradients and their corresponding eigenvalues before 3 months, it is very difficult to tell whether the observed AP gradient indeed evolves into the SA axis or if there are higher dimensional dynamics that underlie this transition. Furthermore, without explicitly considering temporal continuity in the modeling process, it is also difficult to understand how the SA axis gradually comes into existence from the AP axis.
By restricting the analysis to the primary gradient and aligning it to an adult template, the authors may be failing to detect an SA axis that is present but secondary in the perinatal period. To support the claim that the SA gradient is absent rather than merely sub-dominant, the authors must show Gradient 1, Gradient 2, and the corresponding scree plots (eigenvalues) for the <3 month age bins.
Response 1.13: Range can be estimated more robustly using robust statistics for the maximum and minimum, for example by using respectively the 99-th and 1-th percentiles. The examples on two groups with different clustering around the mean sound hypothetical and might not reflect the context of the current work. Range and variance are highly correlated, more so than being complementary.
Response 1.16: The response regarding the T1w/T2w ratio misses the biological constraint. While intensity normalization handles scanner variance, it does not account for the biophysics of neonatal tissue. In the first year of life, extremely high water content and low iron/myelin concentration render the T1w/T2w ratio a poor proxy for myeloarchitecture compared to adults. The lack of correlation between the structural and functional gradient growth axes (Q1.33) is likely a Type II error driven by this metric failure, rather than a true biological decoupling. The authors should discuss this biophysical limitation rather than attributing the null result solely to developmental asynchrony.
Response 1.19: Pipelines customized for specific time periods are not necessarily consistent across time between different cohorts. Cortical meshes can be defined differently and can cause inter-pipeline discrepancies particularly when the meshes are mapped to the sphere for downstream analysis.
For lifespan pipelines, see for example https://doi.org/10.1038/s41551-024-01283-7
Response 1.20: The authors acknowledge the confound that neonates/infants were scanned during sleep while older subjects were awake, but suggest that harmonized preprocessing and large sample sizes mitigate this. This reasoning is flawed. Preprocessing removes noise, but it cannot correct for the fundamental electrophysiological state difference between NREM sleep and wakefulness. The attenuation of the DMN and the alteration of long-range integration are biological signatures of sleep, not artifacts.
If the 'Establishment' phase (Phase II) correlates with the age at which subjects begin scanning while awake, the study may simply be tracking the 'Establishment of Wakefulness.' Large sample sizes do not average out a systematic bias present in ~100% of the cohort at a specific age. The authors must cite literature or provide analysis demonstrating that the S-A gradient topology is invariant to sleep state in infants, or explicitly re-frame Phase II as potentially state-dependent.
Response 1.21: The response does not fully address the concern. Regressing out site effects within age bins removes only mean shifts, not the protocol-specific covariance structure that differs substantially between dHCP, BCP, and HCP. Because the clustering is performed on gradients derived from datasets with different TRs, preprocessing pipelines, SNR profiles, and temporal degrees of freedom, the phase boundaries may still reflect acquisition differences rather than neurodevelopmental transitions.
Moreover, the provided analyses remain qualitative. No quantitative cluster stability metrics (ARI/Rand/NMI, silhouette scores, perturbation tests) are reported, and cohort identity is not tested as a predictor of cluster membership. The equal frequency of 3- vs 4-cluster solutions further indicates instability. As written, the evidence is insufficient to conclude that the three phases are independent of dataset boundaries.
Additional quantitative validation is needed to rule out acquisition-driven structure.
Response 1.25: A Spearman correlation of 0.85 implies that roughly 28% of the variance is unexplained/ inconsistent between the two methods. In the context of mapping subtle developmental shifts in high dimensional topology is not trivial. The authors should not rely solely on the correlation coefficient between these two cases. They must demonstrate that the dimensionality and shape of the embeddings (preferably multiple dimensions) are equivalent between these methods. If the gradient-then-average result yields a more variable result across individuals, that is a relevant biological finding that should be reported and not smoothed over.
Response 1.30: The additional analyses described in the rebuttal help, but they do not yet demonstrate that the three identified “phases” are independent of age-binning choices or cohort boundaries.
First, the individual-level clustering analysis is presented qualitatively, but no quantitative stability metrics (e.g., ARI/Rand/NMI between binned and unbinned cluster assignments) are provided. Without these, it is not possible to evaluate whether the same three clusters truly emerge consistently or whether visual similarity reflects smoothing and alignment decisions.
Second, showing that phases “partially overlap” with cohort inclusion does not address the core concern. The relevant question is whether cohort identity predicts cluster membership once age is controlled. This requires explicit testing (e.g., multinomial regression, χ²/MI tests, or adjusted associations). Simply harmonizing by modeling site as a random effect does not rule out cohort-specific variance structure influencing gradient topology.
Third, the clustering procedure itself remains highly sensitive to K-choice, scaling, and the construction of the age-averaged templates. Without examining cluster stability across K, across random initialization, and across alternative harmonization strategies, the conclusion of three robust phases remains premature.
In short, while the added analyses are useful, the evidence provided does not yet demonstrate that the three clusters reflect genuine neurodevelopmental transitions rather than methodological or cohort-driven structure. Additional quantitative validation is required.
Response 1.31: Thank you for the clarification and for adding a limitation about the adult-derived cognitive reference map. However, I do not feel the concern is fully addressed, and the current text of the Results/Discussion still seems inconsistent with how you now describe this analysis.
You state that the goal was not to infer cognitive functions in younger cohorts, but the manuscript repeatedly interprets the findings as tracking the development and maturation of cognition itself (e.g., “formation and maturation of the cognitive spectrum from basic perception to abstract cognition,” “lifespan trajectory and maturation patterns of the cognitive spectrum along the S-A gradient”). Methodologically, however, what you do is: (i) construct an adult “cognitive spectrum” by ranking NeuroSynth term maps along an adult HCP S-A gradient, and then (ii) project those same adult term maps onto age-specific gradients that have been aligned to an adult S-A template. This can only quantify how much developing gradients converge on an adult functional/cognitive ontology; it cannot support inferences about the intrinsic “cognitive spectrum” in infancy and childhood, where both cognitive repertoire and task structure differ.
Relatedly, I still see a degree of circularity. The adult S-A gradient is used both to define the cognitive reference spectrum (by ordering terms along that axis) and to align all age-specific gradients. Measures such as Dice similarity to the reference map are therefore, to a considerable extent, re-expressions of how closely each age group’s gradients have been forced into an adult S-A framework, rather than an independent test of cognitive organization across development.
In my view, the analysis does not justify strong claims about “lifespan maturation of the cognitive spectrum” or the “formation” of a perception-to-abstract-cognition spectrum across the entire age range. At most, it shows that brain regions which, in adults, are preferentially associated with certain cognitive terms become progressively more organized along an adult S-A axis.
Response 1.35: The authors’ clarification—that they excluded gradient values after computation rather than re-embedding network-ablated matrices—confirms that this analysis is circular. Since the Somatomotor and Default Mode networks are mathematically defined as the anchors (the extremes) of the S-A gradient, "knocking them out" and observing a shift in the mean is a tautological arithmetic certainty, not a biological insight into system "contributions" or "interplay." The results describe the definition of the gradient, not its developmental mechanism. We strongly suggest the authors remove the causal language (e.g., "somatomotor system contributed most significantly") and frame this strictly as a descriptive property of the distribution.
Response 1.39: Thank you for adding the cosine similarity analysis. However, I do not feel this fully addresses my question about alternative template construction, nor the interpretational issues around template choice. First, you explicitly acknowledge that you did not implement alternative template schemes, yet you present the individual→template cosine similarity as evidence that your current scheme “effectively captures age-specific functional topographies.” Because individual gradients are Procrustes-aligned to the age-specific templates before similarity is computed, this metric is not an independent validation of the template but is partly tautological: it will naturally increase with age as SNR and motion improve and as the alignment itself enforces correspondence. Second, I see a tension between this new analysis and your own canonical S-A axis results. In the main text, similarity between group-level gradients and the canonical S-A axis from Sydnor et al. increases in Phase I, decreases in Phase II, and then stabilizes at a high level in Phase III (Supplementary Fig. 2). Yet the individual→age-template similarity in Supplementary Fig. 25 increases through childhood and adolescence and peaks in early adulthood. This divergence suggests that the age-binned template plus multi-step Procrustes procedure may be absorbing the substantial reconfiguration of gradients in infancy–early childhood into the templates themselves, smoothing over the mismatch to an independent canonical SA axis. In my view, this new analysis does not substitute for testing alternative template construction strategies (e.g., different reference ages, pooled templates, or reduced reliance on the adult HCP anchor), nor does it resolve the concern that the developmental story might depend sensitively on the current template choice.
Response 1.40: I appreciate the clarification. However, my concern was less about the number of reported metrics and more about how fully the analysis leverages the rich spatial information in the gradients. Most of the results you describe are based on 1D summary measures (e.g., global range, network-averaged values, bin widths, centile trajectories) rather than analyses of spatial patterning per se (e.g., within-network reconfigurations, local clusters, or multivariate spatial relationships among gradients). In my view, the current work still primarily treats gradients as scalar scores to be summarized across regions and fitted with age-curves, which is different from a deeper topographic analysis of gradient organization. At minimum, I would encourage tempering statements that the S–A gradient provides a full “developmental blueprint,” to reflect this limitation.
Response 1.42: Is there evidence that this is true in infant brains too? If not, some comparison between high resolution and lower resolution gradients should be done during early life to verify.
Response 1.43: In your reply, you state that analyzing eigenspectra is beyond the scope of the current work. I find this problematic. The manuscript repeatedly claims to characterize hierarchical organization across the lifespan, yet there is no quantitative analysis of how the hierarchical series of embedding axes changes with age. Reporting that the first gradient explains ~20% of variance at each age does not address whether the relative importance of the leading axes (e.g., λ₁, λ₂, λ₃, …) shifts over development, nor whether a single axis is adequate to summarize multi-scale reorganization.
While I appreciate that this study focuses on the S–A axis, the dynamics of that axis—particularly in infancy—are tightly coupled to the behavior of the remaining spectrum. Large changes in eigengaps (e.g., λ₁–λ₂, λ₂–λ₃) would directly bear on whether the S–A axis remains a uniquely dominant dimension at all stages, or whether other axes transiently become equally or more informative. At minimum, plotting age-related trajectories of eigengaps at the subject or group level would provide an important sanity check on the assumption that one axis is sufficient.
Given that the eigenvalues underlying the gradients must already be computed in your existing pipeline, this does not seem like an outlandish or technically burdensome request. If such analyses are not performed, I would strongly encourage you to temper claims about “hierarchical organization” being captured by a single S–A gradient across the lifespan, and to state clearly that the multiscale structure of the eigenspectrum remains uncharacterized.
Response 1.47: The appeal to convergence with prior infant studies is reassuring but does not provide direct evidence that pipeline disparities are not contributing to the inflated gradient range in your data, since those studies also rely on infant-specific acquisition and preprocessing choices. Ideally, one would see at least a limited sensitivity analysis (e.g., a subset of infant and/or adult data reprocessed with a common pipeline, or a demonstration that the infant gradient range is robust across reasonable denoising choices or after controlling for motion and temporal SNR). If such analyses are not feasible within the scope of the current revision, I would encourage you to soften the claim that preprocessing differences cannot systematically bias the gradients and to more explicitly acknowledge this as a limitation when interpreting the inflated infant extremes.
Response 1.51: I appreciate the clarification about the use of NbClust and the suite of clustering indices. However, my original concern was not only how K was chosen, but also about (i) seeing at least some of the underlying metrics (e.g., silhouette widths or gap statistic across candidate K) and (ii) the stability of the “lifespan phases” across different age binning schemes. The current response does not address the bin-width stability, and the NbClust results are only summarized qualitatively.
Response 1.55: Please include a statement in the manuscript to reflect that this study is performed in compliance with the NDA data use agreement.
(Remarks on code availability)
The code suggests a potential flaw in the implementation; see the “General Comments” section of my report for details.
Reviewer #2
(Remarks to the Author)
I commend the authors on their efforts to address all reviewer comments through substantial and insightful additional analyses. The inclusion of these new analyses has provided a much more thorough description of the data and has added confidence that the overall patterns of results are not substantively impacted by different analytic choices. This leaves the authors with the difficult task of synthesizing and interpreting the expanded corpus of results into a cohesive story. I feel this part is somewhat incomplete, leaving important food for thought on the table. Sharpening the story in light of all the new analyses could help to improve the impact of this huge body of work. I mention a few of these areas below.
Sex effects observed in the new analyses are surprising and bear further scrutiny. There should be some discussion of these findings. There is currently no reference to this analysis or finding in the main text of the manuscript. Rather than burying these results in the supplement, the paper would be strengthened by referencing them directly in the text and offering an interpretation or discussion of their potential meaning in the discussion section
The flip in gradient dominance during phase 2 (e.g. Supplementary Figure 1) and the corresponding dip in correlation of the primary gradient and the canonical SA axis (Supplementary Figure 2) is quite interesting. It seems that something unique and important going on during phase II that may be developmentally reorganizing the A-P gradient into what will eventually become the S-A gradient by means of a dominance of gradient 2. The authors discuss possible reasons for the S-A gradient emergence in general in the discussion, but some additional interpretation of what is going on during this unique period, and what it means for “principal” vs secondary gradients during development—and these sorts of PCA approaches in general—would be useful to explore more.
Some of the spatial correlation plots appear to actually have non-linear relationships, yet they are always analyzed and overlaid with a linear fit (e.g Fig 3g, Supplementary Fig 9a). I am left wondering if appreciating this non-linearity would be meaningful for understanding how all the pieces fit together.
(Remarks on code availability)
The code appears to be documented and complete; however, I did not try to execute it so cannot comment on whether it can be run successfully.
Reviewer #3
(Remarks to the Author)
My comments have been addressed. I have no further comments.
(Remarks on code availability)

## Paper

## Abstract

The human cortical functional hierarchy, spanning from primary sensorimotor to transmodal association regions, represents a fundamental principle of brain organization. Here, we show lifespan changes in the sensorimotor-association (S-A) gradient in the cortical functional hierarchy using multimodal neuroimaging data from 33,247 participants aged 32 postmenstrual weeks to 80 years. We identify three critical neurodevelopmental milestones: initiation (third trimester to perinatal period), establishment (infancy to early childhood), and expansion-stabilization (late childhood to adulthood). Pronounced gradient changes are predominantly observed during the first decade, with continued refinement extending into mid-adulthood. Spatiotemporally heterogeneous growth patterns in functional gradients align with evolutionary hierarchies, segregation–integration dynamics, structural maturation, and cognitive spectrum development, proceeding along a dominant S-A growth axis. These findings establish a unified neurodevelopmental framework that links connectome gradient dynamics to multifaceted functional and structural properties, advancing our understanding of cortical hierarchy maturation across the lifespan.

---

## Introduction

The functional hierarchy in the human cerebral cortex serves as a fundamental principle of brain organization. At the macroscale, functional connectome gradients provide a critical framework for delineating the intrinsic spatial topography of the brain 1,2. Among these gradients, the sensorimotor-association (S-A) gradient represents the principal axis of the cortical functional hierarchy, spanning from primary and unimodal regions to transmodal association regions 3. This gradient axis is anchored at its extremes by the most distal cortical regions, with multimodal regions occupying intermediate positions along the continuum 1,3,4. This cortex-wide organization ensures the spatial continuity of information transfer across adjacent areas, facilitating a continuous cognitive spectrum ranging from basic sensory processing, perception, and motor action to abstract cognition along the cortical mantle 3,5. Notably, the S-A gradient axis aligns with spatial variations in key neurobiological properties 2, including cortical thickness 6,7, intracortical myelination 8–10, and gene expression signatures 11,12. Perturbations in this hierarchical organization along the S-A axis have been linked to the pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric disorders 13–17. However, despite its central role in cortical organization, the spatiotemporal dynamics of S-A axis across the lifespan, as well as its coevolution with multifaceted structural properties, remain poorly understood. Addressing these knowledge gaps is essential for advancing our understanding of the principles governing cortical functional organization and their implications for both normative cognition and the pathogenesis of neuropsychiatric disorders.

The development patterns of the S-A axis have garnered considerable interests 16,18–23. Emerging evidence suggests that the anterior–posterior gradient configuration begins to form during prenatal development 18,19, manifesting as an immature S-A hierarchy. Although the S-A axis becomes discernible during preschool years 16, its global and regional topography undergoes gradual refinement throughout childhood and adolescence 20,21, continuing into adulthood 22,23. This protracted process facilitates progressive segregation and integration, supporting the emergence of advanced cognitive abilities 19,20. Despite these advances, critical gaps remain in the lifespan maturation of the functional hierarchy. First, most existing studies of the functional hierarchy have focused on discrete developmental stages (e.g., the third trimester 19, neonatal period 18, adolescence 20,21 and adulthood 3,22), resulting in a fragmented perspective that obscures nonlinear gradient dynamics across the full age continuum. Moreover, prior work has often been limited by small (e.g., N < 100) 18,19 or modest (N = hundreds to thousands) 16,20–22 sample sizes, along with a predominant reliance on linear modelling for gradient development 19,20,22. Although a recent study 23 established a continuous, nonlinear mapping of functional gradients from birth to 100 years of age, the developmental patterns remain constrained by a modest sample size (N = 3,556) and particularly sparse data coverage during childhood. Second, previous studies have failed to delineate how functional hierarchies coevolve with specific structural and geometric features, such as cortical thickness 2,6,7, intracortical myelination 2,8,9, and intrinsic geometry 3,24, across the lifespan. While the S-A axis aligns spatially with these structural attributes in adult brains, the developmental functional-structural synchrony remains unclear. A previous study 23 linked lifespan changes in functional gradients with a composite structural gradient, but its analysis strategy that integrates multiple structural features into a morphometric similarity network, did not directly assess how specific structural properties shape functional gradients. Therefore, addressing these fundamental questions will require large-scale, lifespan-spanning multimodal neuroimaging datasets, harmonized processing pipelines and non-linear analytical frameworks capable of modelling lifespan trajectories of functional gradients, structural properties, and their dynamic interactions.

To address these challenges, we utilized multimodal neuroimaging data from 33,247 participants aged between 32 postmenstrual weeks (PMW) and 80 years, collected at 132 global sites. By employing a diffusion map embedding approach 3,25, we identified the S-A gradient of the functional connectome. Specifically, we sought to i) delineate neurodevelopmental milestones of the spatial organization and extent of the S-A gradient axis, ii) map nonlinear trajectories of the S-A axis at the global, system, and regional levels via generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS) 26, iii) investigate how lifespan changes in the functional gradient axis correlate with multifaceted structural and geometric hierarchies, and iv) conduct a NeuroSynth-based meta-analysis 27 to examine the alignment of developing S-A gradient with adult cognitive spectrum. These integrative multimodal and multifaceted analyses provide insights into the principles governing the lifespan maturation of the cortical hierarchy.

## Results

Following a rigorous quality control protocol 28, we analyzed structural MRI and task-free functional MRI data from 33,247 participants aged 32 PMW and 80 years. Detailed demographic information, acquisition parameters, quality control procedures, and preprocessing protocols are described in the Methods section and in our prior work 28. Preprocessed functional data were mapped onto cortical surfaces, and functional connectomes were constructed by computing pairwise correlation coefficients between the time series of all cortical surface vertices (4,609 × 4,609) 28. Using well-established diffusion map embedding techniques 3,25, we decomposed both age-specific, group-level connectomes and person-specific connectomes into multiple gradients representing functional connectivity variations across the brain. Our primary focus was on the lifespan growth of the principal S-A gradient, given its pivotal role in cognition 3, development 19–21,29, disease 13–17, and evolution 30,31.

Topographically distinct growth stages of the S-A gradient axis
We investigated whether the S-A gradient undergoes distinct stages across the lifespan using both group- and individual-level analyses. We first examined how the hierarchical S-A axis emerges during early development and matures into a canonical gradient of cortical functional organization. To this end, we divided the lifespan into 26 distinct age groups 28 and generated 26 age-specific, group-based functional connectomes. Age ranges were defined with finer intervals for early developmental stages, reflecting rapid changes, and broader intervals for adulthood, reflecting relative stability. Initially, the connectome gradient manifests as an anterior‒posterior axis, which gradually evolves into the canonical S-A axis that spans from primary and unimodal regions at one end to transmodal frontal, temporal, and parietal association regions at the other end (Fig. 1a). This maturation process highlights substantial reorganization of the functional topography of the S-A axis over the lifespan. To delineate the temporal sequence of S-A axis establishment and maturation, we performed K-means clustering analysis on the 26 group-based gradient maps (Fig. 1b & Supplementary Fig. 1). This analysis revealed that functional gradients across age groups are optimally clustered into three distinct stages (Fig. 1b, c).

i) Phase I: Initiation. This phase covers the third trimester and perinatal period (approximately 32 PMW to 1 month). During this stage, cortical topography begins to differentiate functionally between anterior and posterior regions, accompanied by a gradual broadening of the gradient range (Fig. 1a, d).

ii) Phase II: Establishment. Spanning infancy to early childhood (approximately 3 months to 4 years), this phase is characterized by a remarkable transition in functional topography, as the anterior‒posterior gradient is replaced by the S-A gradient (Fig. 1a, d). Early in infancy (approximately 3‒9 months), the anterior‒posterior gradient range narrows, and multiple peaks emerge along this axis (Fig. 1a, d), reflecting increased functional differentiation in cortical organization. By late infancy and early childhood (approximately 12 months to 4 years), the canonical S-A axis is established, as evidenced by two distinct peaks in the ridge distribution corresponding to the sensorimotor and association cortices, respectively (Fig. 1a, d).

iii) Phase III: Expansion and stability. This phase extends from late childhood through adolescence and adulthood (5 years to 80 years). During late childhood and adolescence, the cortical topography of the S-A gradient becomes clearly discernible and undergoes progressive expansion in the gradient range, followed by a prolonged period of relative stability in cortical topography over several decades (Fig. 1a, c, and d). Notably, it is during adolescence that the S-A gradient solidifies as the dominant principal gradient (Supplementary Fig. 2).

We also mapped the visual-sensorimotor (V-S) and the modulation-representation (M-R) gradients maps across the lifespan. The V-S gradient emerges from an early anterior-posterior pattern before birth and refines progressively from infancy through adulthood. In contrast, the M-R gradient is preliminarily established by early childhood and gradually stabilizes into its mature configuration during adolescence and adulthood (Supplementary Fig. 3-4). We further computed the spatial similarity between these group-specific gradients and the canonical S-A axis2 and observed that it increased steadily with age in Phase I, slightly decreased in Phase II, and eventually stabilized at a high level in Phase III (Supplementary Fig. 5). Notably, the slight decrease observed during Phase II is accompanied by a period of transient instability in cortical gradient organization, during which the dorsal attention (DA) and ventral attention (VA) systems show temporary changes in their alignment with large-scale gradients, consistent with broader shifts in gradient organization (Supplementary Fig. 6). This trend supports the view that the S-A axis is not fully established at birth but rather emerges through progressive reorganization. The three developmental phases were also identified through individual-level gradient clustering without predefined age bins, within-age-group-harmonized analysis, and within-dataset replication analyses (Supplementary Fig. 7-11). Nonetheless, the definitions and age boundaries of developmental phases could be influenced by methodological choices such as site effects and clustering analysis.

Normative growth of the S-A gradient axis across lifespan
We systematically delineated the lifespan growth trajectories of the S-A gradient at the global, system and regional levels. Lifespan growth curves were modelled using GAMLSS 26, with age included as a smoothing term, sex and in-scanner head motion as fixed effects, and site as a random effect. The growth rates were derived as the first derivatives of these growth curves.

i) Global level. Three global gradient measures 14 were evaluated for the S-A axis: the explanation ratio, which measures the percentage of variance in the connectivity profile accounted for by the gradient; the gradient range, which measures the difference between the two extremes of the gradient; and the standard deviation, which measures the heterogeneity of gradient values across the cortex. The explanation ratio of the S-A gradient exhibited a prolonged period of nonlinear increase, peaking in the late fifth decade (46.8 years, 95% bootstrap confidence interval (CI): 43.4-49.9), followed by a gradual decline (Fig. 2a). Similarly, both the gradient range and standard deviation of the S-A axis demonstrated nonlinear increases, peaking in the fourth decade (gradient range: 32.0 years, 95% bootstrap CI: 29.2-36.1; standard deviation: 36.2 years, 95% bootstrap CI: 33.9-38.8; Fig. 2a).

ii) System level. We examined the lifespan growth trajectories of the gradient range, standard deviation, and gradient values for each system within the S-A axis. Here, individual-level functional systems were derived by integrating age-specific Yeo 7-network atlases with a person-specific iterative algorithm 28,32,33. Generally, the growth curves for the gradient range and standard deviation across all brain systems (Fig. 2b) mirrored the patterns observed at the global level (Fig. 2a). Notably, the default-mode network (DMN) and frontoparietal network (FPN) exhibited higher gradient ranges and standard deviations, whereas the sensorimotor systems presented lower values throughout the lifespan, reflecting greater functional differentiation in association cortices than in primary cortices. Gradient value analysis revealed distinct nonlinear growth patterns across systems (Supplementary Fig. 12). Specifically, the visual, ventral attention, and dorsal attention systems reach their extreme values during adolescence, whereas the DMN, FPN, and somatomotor systems exhibited more protracted trajectories, reaching their extreme values in the fourth decade of life (Fig. 2c). To further characterize the distribution of gradient values across systems along the S‑ A axis, we performed a descriptive exclusion analysis by iteratively removing each system's vertices and quantifying the shift in mean gradient value normalized by vertex count. This analysis revealed system-specific differences in gradient distribution across developmental stages (repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA), F (12,199460) = 341.8, p < 0.001; Fig. 2d and Supplementary Tables 1-4). During Phase I and Phase II, excluding somatomotor-associated vertices produced the largest shifts in the mean gradient value (all post-hoc ps < 0.001), whereas during Phase III, the largest shifts resulted from excluding DMN-associated vertices (all post-hoc ps < 0.001).

iii) Regional level. We characterized the regional maturation processes of gradient values along the S-A axis. The most pronounced changes occurring in the first decade of life and continued into at least early adulthood (Fig. 2e). Notably, substantial changes in regional gradient values were observed not only at the two extremes of the S-A axis (e.g., posterior DMN and lateral visual regions), but also at intermediate positions (e.g., ventral attention regions such as the insula and dorsal anterior cingulate, and dorsal attention regions such as the superior frontal and parietal cortices). To elucidate the spatiotemporal growth principles across the cortex, we applied principal component analysis (PCA) to the fitted growth curves of all vertices. The first principal component accounted for 65.4% of the variance in the regional gradient profiles (Fig. 2f), representing the dominant lifespan growth axis. Along this axis, distinct growth patterns of gradient values were evident in the sensorimotor and association cortices (Fig. 2f). This dominant lifespan growth axis closely aligned with the S-A gradient axis (Spearman’s ρ = 0.91, p < 0.001; Supplementary Fig. 13) and the macaque-to-human evolutionary hierarchy (Spearman’s ρ = 0.32, p = 0.02; Fig. 2g).

Lifespan association between the S-A axis and segregation/integration
The hierarchical organization of cortical architecture facilitates efficient information transfer between sensorimotor and association regions 4, which is critically dependent on the dynamic equilibrium between functional segregation and integration 34. Here, we investigated the lifespan coupling between S-A gradient and segregation-integration dynamics via graph theoretical analysis. Our findings revealed that the global clustering coefficient (C , segregation index) and inverse characteristic shortest path length (1/L , integration index) exhibited distinct nonlinear maturation trajectories: the C demonstrated an initial increase, peaking in early adulthood (32.7 years, 95% bootstrap CI: 30.7–35.0), followed by a gradual decline (Fig. 3a), whereas 1/L p showed an initial decease, reaching its minimum in mid-adulthood (41.1 years, 95% bootstrap CI: 39.6–42.7), before subsequently increasing (Fig. 3b).

Regional clustering coefficient (C ) decreased from primary to transmodal association regions, independent of age (Fig. 3c). While sensorimotor regions presented the highest levels of local clustering throughout the cortex, these primary regions still presented a nonlinear increase in functional specialization from infancy through early adulthood, followed by a decline in later aging stages (Fig. 3c). Regional efficiency (1/L ) demonstrated substantial developmental changes primarily during the first decade of life: sensorimotor regions exhibited peak efficiency during infancy, which gradually decreased with development, whereas association regions showed marked increases in efficiency, becoming dominant from childhood through adolescence and adulthood (Fig. 3d). This pattern reflects a developmental trajectory of reduced integration in primary regions alongside enhanced integration in association regions as functional specialization progresses. Spatial correlation analyses revealed significant associations between clustering coefficient maps and functional gradient maps across the lifespan (all p < 0.05, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 14a), whereas regional efficiency showed no significant correlations (all p > 0.05, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 14b). This finding suggests that functional gradient maturation is more strongly coupled with functional segregation than with integration.

Finally, we applied PCA to the fitted growth curves of regional clustering (C ) and efficiency (1/L ) values across all vertices. The first PCA components accounted for 74.9% and 57.6% of the variance in the regional clustering and efficiency growth profiles, respectively (Fig. 3e, f). Notably, both regional clustering and efficiency demonstrated spatially heterogeneous maturation patterns across the lifespan. The lifespan S-A growth axes of regional clustering and efficiency were correlated with those of the canonical connectome gradient (regional clustering: Spearman’s ρ= -0.78, p < 0.001; Fig. 3g; regional efficiency: Spearman’s ρ= 0.19, p = 0.02; Fig. 3h).

To complement the graph-theoretical results, we additionally examined averaged within- and between-system FC across vertices 35,36. Both measures showed systematic variation along the S-A axis and were significantly coupled with S-A gradient maturation across the lifespan (Supplementary Fig. 15-16). PCA further revealed that developmental axes of both measures were correlated with the growth axis of the S-A gradient (within-system FC: Spearman’s ρ= -0.51, p < 0.001; between-system FC: Spearman’s ρ= -0.56, p < 0.001; Supplementary Fig. 15). These findings highlight that the lifespan maturation of the S-A gradient and functional segregation/integration proceed in a convergent manner along an overarching, hierarchical growth axis.

Lifespan association between the S-A axis and structural hierarchies
We investigated how the S-A gradient axis coevolves with multifaceted geometric and structural features across the lifespan. Our investigation focused on three features: geometric distance 3,24, macrostructural cortical thickness 7, and intracortical T1w/T2w contrast ratio 9.

For geometric distance analysis, we first identified vertices within the top and bottom 5% of S-A gradient values (Fig. 4a), representing regions of maximal functional differentiation. For each individual, we calculated the mean normalized geometric distances between paired vertices with extreme gradient values. This geometric distance exhibited a nonlinear trajectory across the lifespan, peaking during young adulthood (20.7 years, 95% bootstrap CI: 17.2–23.2), followed by a gradual decline (Fig. 4b). Cosine similarity analysis between geometric distances and gradient value differences revealed robust geometry–hierarchy coupling (r > 0.88 across all ages), with similarity decreasing until late adolescence (peak at 17.0 years, 95% bootstrap CI: 14.3-19.5) and stabilizing thereafter (Fig. 4c). These findings suggest that while geometric constraints strongly influence the functional hierarchy, their influence gradually diminishes during development.

For structural analyses, our investigation revealed the following key findings: First, transmodal association cortices exhibited greater cortical thickness and reduced T1w/T2w contrast ratio than did sensorimotor cortices throughout the lifespan (Fig. 4d, e), which is consistent with established S-A axis characteristics in adults7,10. Structural changes were most pronounced during the first decade of life and continued into the third decade, with distinct regional patterns: cortical thinning predominated in transmodal association cortices, whereas the primary visual cortex showed thickening (Fig. 4d), and T1w/T2w contrast ratio patterns revealed decreased levels in paralimbic association cortices (e.g., insula and dorsal anterior cingulate) alongside increased levels in sensorimotor regions (Fig. 4e). Second, spatial correlation analyses revealed significant associations between functional gradient maps and both cortical thickness and intracortical T1w/T2w contrast ratio maps across the lifespan (all p < 0.05, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 17), with the strongest correlations occurring during the first two decades. Third, PCA of the structural growth curves revealed that the first principal components explained 97.3% and 89.0% of the variance in the cortical thickness and intracortical T1w/T2w contrast ratio growth profiles, respectively (Fig. 4f, g). The cortical thickness growth axis exhibited a regionally heterogeneous pattern spanning from sensorimotor to association cortices (Fig. 4f), with a positive correlation with the functionally defined S-A growth axis (Spearman’s ρ= 0.36, p < 0.001; Fig. 4h). In contrast, the T1w/T2w contrast ratio-based growth axis extended from the sensorimotor cortices to paralimbic association cortices (e.g., the insula and cingulate cortex) (Fig. 4g) and was not correlated with either the lifespan growth axis of the functional gradient (Spearman’s ρ = 0.04, p = 0.42; Fig. 4i) or the cortical thickness (Spearman’s ρ = 0.01, p = 0.25). These findings collectively demonstrate that lifespan maturation of functional gradients is primarily coupled with cytoarchitectural development rather than myeloarchitectural development.

Lifespan S-A gradient alignment with adult cognitive spectrum
In adults, the S-A gradient axis supports a cognitive spectrum that spans from perception and action to abstract cognition 3. However, how lifespan changes in the S–A axis align with this adult cognitive spectrum remains unknown. To address this issue, we conducted a cognitive decoding meta-analysis on both group- and person-specific S-A gradients in the NeuroSynth database 27. The dominant S-A gradient was first identified from young adult Human connectome project data (n=897) 37. We then constructed a reference spectrum map comprising 24 cognitive terms distributed along the S-A axis (for details, see Methods). This reference map showed a clear continuum: perception and action terms anchored the primary/unimodal end, while abstract cognitive terms dominated the transmodal end (Fig. 5a), replicating earlier findings 3.

For group-level analysis, we generated cognitive spectrum maps along the S-A axis for each of the 26 age-specific groups via identical procedures to those used for reference map construction (Fig. 5a). We quantified two key metrics: i) the mean gradient bin width associated with cognitive terms, reflecting the degree of clustering of the corresponding brain areas along the S-A axis, and ii) the correlation between the median gradient bin of each term and its corresponding gradient percentile, reflecting the covariation between the cognitive and S-A axes (Fig. 5b, left panel). Our analyses revealed that compared with those of earlier developmental stages, Phase III (expansion and stability stage) presented narrower mean gradient widths (Kruskal‒Wallis test, η2 = 0.62, p < 0.001; post-hoc tests, both p ≤ 0.01; Fig. 5b, middle panel) and stronger cognitive‒gradient correlations (Kruskal‒Wallis test, η2 = 0.73, p < 0.001; post-hoc both p ≤ 0.002; Fig. 5b, right panel). Individual-level analysis of the cognitive spectrum maps revealed that the mean term width decreased rapidly during early development and stabilized after adolescence (peak at 15.3 years, 95% bootstrap CI: 14.5‒16.6; Fig. 5c), whereas the cognitive term‒gradient correlations increased progressively, reaching maximal values in the third decade of life (29.3 years, 95% bootstrap CI: 26.1‒31.8; Fig. 5c). Finally, quantitative comparison of group-based cognitive spectrum maps with the reference map via Dice coefficients revealed a progressive increase in similarity from the perinatal period through early adulthood, followed by a modest decline (Fig. 5d). Individual-level analysis revealed a similar developmental trajectory, with Dice coefficient peaking in the third decade (26.1 years, 95% bootstrap CI: 25.4‒28.7; Fig. 5e). These results reveal a progressive strengthening of alignment between age-specific functional gradients and the adult cognitive spectrum, reflecting the developmental convergence of cortical organization toward adult cognitive-functional topography.

Sex differences in the lifespan S-A gradient
To investigate sex differences in the lifespan trajectory of the S-A gradient axis, we fitted GAMLSS models with a sex-by-age interaction term at the global, system, and regional levels. Globally, females showed higher explanation ratio and greater gradient range and variation across the lifespan than males (all p < 0.05, FDR-corrected, Supplementary Fig. 18a). At the system level, females also showed greater gradient ranges and variations than males (all p < 0.001, FDR-corrected, Supplementary Fig. 18b). Notably, in several systems, including visual, limbic, FPN, and DMN, females exhibited later peak ages than males (all p < 0.001, FDR-corrected, Supplementary Fig. 18c and Supplementary Table 5). Regionally, females showed higher gradient values in medial prefrontal and parietal regions and later temporal regions, whereas males exhibited higher values in the occipital regions (p < 0.001, FDR-corrected, Supplementary Fig. 18d). These findings indicate that sex differences in cortical hierarchy manifest not only in magnitude but also in developmental timing.

Sensitivity analyses
To validate the lifespan growth patterns of the S-A gradient, we conducted a comprehensive sensitivity analysis via the following five strategies 28 (for details, see Methods and Supplementary Fig 19-24): i) To minimize the influence of head motion, we replicated the main analysis via data from 24,494 participants with a stricter motion threshold (mFD < 0.2 mm). ii) To assess the potential effects of sampling, we performed 1,000 bootstrap resampling iterations. iii) To evaluate the reproducibility of our results, we implemented a split-half replication strategy. iv) To examine the potential influence of specific sites, we performed leave-one-site-out analyses. v) To address biases from unbalanced sample sizes and site distributions across age groups, we employed a balanced resampling approach (1,000 times). The results of these sensitivity analyses were statistically compared with the main results. At the global and system levels, all the growth curves strongly correlated with the main results (global measures: Pearson’s r =0.99±0.01, MSE=9.5×10-5±1.7×10-4; Fig. 6a; system-level measures: Pearson’s r =0.98±0.03, MSE=3.5×10-5±5.5×10-4; Fig. 6b). The peak ages of gradient values for each system identified in the validation results closely aligned with those observed in the main results (mean standard deviation age = 0.91 years; Fig. 6c). All sensitivity analyses replicated system-based exclusion results (Fig. 6d and Supplementary Table 6). The regional lifespan growth rate of the S-A gradient was highly consistent across analytical strategies: 95.4% of vertices showed intraclass correlation coefficient values greater than 0.5 and the overall minimum mean square error (MMSE) remained low (< 5 × 10-6) (Fig. 6e). Furthermore, the lifespan growth axis showed strong consistency across strategies (r = 0.97 ± 0.01), with each strategy clearly differentiating the S-A axis (Fig. 6f).

To evaluate the influence of sample size, we conducted a resampling-based sensitivity analysis across sample sizes ranging from 200 to 33,000 participants. Both mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) decreased as sample size increased (Supplementary Fig. 25). Notably, errors at the global and system levels declined sharply until approximately 5,000 participants, after which further reductions plateaued. Regionally, a sample size of ~6,000 participants was required to achieve stable error estimates for more than half of cortical vertices, while a quarter of vertices demanded even larger samples. This analysis indicates that larger samples are essential for reliable gradient growth curves and offers practical guidance for future lifespan neuroimaging studies.
