Q1.9 Anterior-posterior gradient during early infancy – This is contradictory to previous observation that the SA gradient already exists at birth. The SA gradient does not start to occur at 3 months but before that.
R: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment and the opportunity to clarify. In our data, we observed a prominent anterior-posterior (A-P) gradient during the prenatal and neonatal periods, which progressively transitions into a more differentiated S-A gradient after approximately 3 months of age. This observation of an A-P gradient in early infancy is consistent with prior studies. For instance, Xia et al. (2024) reported the emergence of an anterior-posterior gradient as early as 34.6 postmenstrual weeks 1. Lariviere et al. (2020) described anterior-posterior variations in term-born neonates, interpreting these as an immature precursor of the differentiation between unimodal and transmodal areas 2.
The apparent inconsistency with Ref23 likely reflects methodological differences. Specifically, Ref23 employed a generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) to fit gradient development across the entire age range. Given the brevity of the early developmental window and the relatively small sample size available, such modeling may smooth or shape the less differentiated early-stage patterns into a more continuous S-A trajectory. In contrast, our approach used group-level analyses within discrete age bins, enabling us to directly characterize gradient architecture at each developmental stage without imposing model-based continuity across age. We have revised the text by adding a small discussion (page 18):
“Notably, we found that the functional topography at birth is not characterized by the S-A gradient but is instead dominated by an anterior-posterior differentiation. This finding is aligned with previous studies of preterm, term-born, and neonatal cohorts 18,19, suggesting that this pattern represents a developmental precursor to the mature S-A gradient. In contrast, one recent study 23 suggests that the S-A gradient is already present at birth. The discrepancy may partly arise from methodological differences: the previous study 23 applied lifespan generalized additive mixed modeling, which could smooth over less differentiated early-stage patterns. Our stage-specific analyses, by comparison, capture gradient organization directly at each period, offering a more fine-grained characterization of early functional topography.”
Q1.10 Grouping the broad age range from 5 years to 80 years as a single phase (Phase III) is too coarse and does not reflect the fact that growth inflection points happen quite often during adolescence.
R: We would like to further clarify this point. Our analysis for defining Phase III was not to suggest that age span from 5 to 80 years constitutes a homogenous developmental stage. Rather, Phase III was conceptualized as a broader period of gradient stabilization and refinement-a stage in which the S-A gradient, once established, undergoes progressive fine-tuned throughout childhood, adolescence, and adulthood, and then continues to evolve into late life. We have clarified this point in the revised manuscript (page 19):
“our definition of Phase III (5-80 years) reflects the prolonged refinement and stabilization of the S-A gradient from childhood, adolescence to adulthood, rather than developmental uniformity through this period.”

R: To ensure consistency across datasets, we converted gestational age in the dHCP dataset into chronological age by treating 40 gestational weeks as the time of birth (i.e., 0 years). Chronological age was then calculated as:

𝐶ℎ𝑟𝑜𝑛𝑜𝑙𝑜𝑔𝑖𝑐𝑎𝑙 𝑎𝑔𝑒 (𝑦𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑠)=

The conversion was based on the assumption that 40 gestational weeks corresponds to birth (0 years of chronological age). Q1.12 “Collectively, these results revealed previously unreported spatiotemporal patterns and critical neurodevelopmental milestones of the functional hierarchy, as characterized by the initiation, establishment, and expansion/stability of the S-A axis of cortical functional organization.” Again, this is untrue in light of ref 23.
R: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. The related statements have been removed from the revised version.
Q1.13 Range and variance are measuring almost the same thing, i.e., the spread of the gradient values, and are therefore redundant. Please pick one to report.
R: While both range and standard deviation quantify aspects of distribution spread, they emphasize distinct properties. The range captures the full extent of gradient differentiation (maximum-minimum), highlighting the span of the axis and sensitivity to extreme values. In contrast, the standard deviation reflects the average dispersion of all gradient values (not just the maximum and minimum) around the mean, providing a more robust, outlier-resistant measure of variability. For example, consider two groups of numbers with the same range: one group is tightly clustered around the mean, and the other is spread out more evenly between the minimum and maximum values. Both groups have the same range, but the first group will have a smaller standard deviation, indicating less variability around the mean, whereas the second group will have a larger standard deviation, reflecting greater dispersion. Because these two indices offer complementary perspectives‒one emphasizing the maximal differentiation and the other overall dispersion‒we report both to provide a fuller characterization of developmental and topographical features of the gradient.
Q1.14 In Figure 2c and throughout the paper, it is unclear what “gradient score” is referring to.
R: To improve clarity, we have revised the terminology throughout the manuscript and figure legends, replacing “gradient score” with “gradient value”. This change more accurately reflects the numerical values derived from the gradient decomposition.
Q1.15 The results shown in Figure 2e seem to indicate that the SA gradient changes very little after 20 years. This contradicts Figs 2a and 2b and other results shown in the paper.
R: We would like to make a clarification about this point. First, the apparent stability of the S-A gradient after age 20 in Fig. 2e was partly due to the original colormap design rather than the underlying results. Specifically, the broad white center of the colormap compressed the visual contrast around zero values, making age-related changes less discernible. In the revised figure (see updated Fig. 2e), we applied a colormap with more balanced contrast to better capture subtle variations across adulthood.
Second, our analyses do indicate that the S-A gradient continues to change after early adulthood, although at a slower rate compared with the rapid alterations observed in early childhood. These adult changes are consistent with the global- and system-level results shown in Fig 2a and 2b, which demonstrate relative stabilization of gradient measures from the third decade onward to early aging, while still exhibiting gradual refinements at the regional levels.

Q1.16 T1-weighted and T2-weighted images are not quantitative and can have arbitrary signal gains associated with different scanners, sequences, and choices of acquisition parameters. It is unclear how this is dealt with in this study, which involves datasets from quite a number of different sources.
R: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. It is indeed true that T1-weighted and T2-weighted images are not inherently quantitative, and their signal intensities can vary across scanners, sequences, and acquisition protocols.
Nevertheless, the T1w/T2w ratio provides a reliable proxy for relative cortical myelin content because myelin consistently shortens T1 relaxation times (increasing T1w signal) and T2 relaxation times (decreasing T2w signal), producing a systematic contrast that is amplified when taking their ratio 6,7. This approach has been widely adopted in developmental, clinical and comparative studies 6,8–11. Importantly, several studies have demonstrated that the T1w/T2w ratio produces robust and anatomically meaningful spatial patterns that remain consistent across different scanners and acquisition settings. For example, Glasser et al. reported that group-average datasets acquired on different scanners with different sequences at independent sites yielded qualitatively very similar results 6,7.
In the present study, we took several steps to further mitigate site-related variability. First, during preprocessing we applied biases and intensity normalization, which reduce transmit field biases and minimize intensity inhomogeneities. These steps are critical for improving cross-site comparability of T1w/T2w-derived myelin maps. Second, in our statistical modeling, we explicitly included site as a random effect in the GAMLSS framework, thereby adjusting for potential residual site-specific differences when estimating growth trajectories.
Together, these strategies substantially reduce concerns regarding inter-scanner variability and support the robustness of our T1w/T2w-based myelin estimates across multiple datasets. In the revised manuscript, we have added relevant description and hopefully it is clearer now (page 29).
“To mitigate inter-scanner variability and enhance cross-site comparability, all T1w and T2w images underwent bias correction and intensity normalization prior to the computation of the T1w/T2w ratio.……. we fitted the growth curves of the structural attributes for each vertex via GAMLSS with age and sex as fixed effects, and site as a random effect.”
Q1.17 Were the inter-vertex geometric distances normalized with respect to the “total” inter-vertex distance. Since the brain is changing in size across the lifespan, it is unclear how the brain size will affect the analysis on geometric distance.
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. To account for inter-individual differences in brain size and their potential impact on geodesic distance measures, we normalized geodesic distances by the square root of the cortical surface area. This was done when analyzing distances between vertices within the top and bottom 5% of S-A gradient values. We then re-fitted the lifespan growth curves using these normalized distances, and the results remained highly consistent with our original findings. We have rephrased the relevant sections in Methods and Results as follows:
Methods (page 28): “To account for inter-individual differences in brain size, geodesic distances were normalized by the square root of the cortical surface area.”
Results (page 12): “For each individual, we calculated the mean normalized geometric distances between paired vertices with extreme gradient values. This geometric distance exhibited a nonlinear trajectory across the lifespan, peaking during young adulthood (20.7 years, 95% bootstrap CI: 17.2–23.2), followed by a gradual decline (Fig. 4b).”
Q1.18 Why multi-step Procrustes alignment using age groups, instead of constructing the gradient template directly from the gradients of the individuals?
R: We adopted a multi-step Procrustes alignment based on age groups to reduce potential biases arising from sample size imbalances and age-related variations in gradient topography. If a group-level gradient template were constructed directly from all individual embeddings, the resulting template would likely be disproportionately influenced by age groups with larger sample size and might obscure meaningful developmental stage-specific differences. By first aligning gradients within narrower age groups and then iteratively converging toward a common template, our approach ensures that the reference template captures both shared organizational features and age-specific variations in gradient topography. This strategy provides a more balanced and representative framework for comparing gradients across the lifespan. We have rephrased the relevant sections (page 23):
“To ensure accurate comparisons between groups, we applied Procrustes rotation 79 to align age-specific group-level functional gradients to iterative group-level reference gradients……Compared with constructing the template directly from individual gradients, this multi-step alignment strategy reduces biases from sample size imbalances and development variations in gradient topography.”
Q1.19 Cortical surfaces were generated using different pipelines and hence cortical thickness measurements are not consistent. For example, iBEAT surfaces and FreeSurfer might not be entirely consistent. The conclusions might be affected by this inconsistency.
R: We used different cortical surface reconstruction pipelines for different age groups (iBEAT for infants and FreeSurfer for older participants). This decision was intentional 12–14, as each tool has been specifically optimized for the developmental stage it targets. Applying a single pipeline across the entire age range would likely introduce greater bias, since adult-oriented tools such as FreeSurfer are suboptimal for infant brains, while infant-tailored pipelines are not designed for adult anatomy.
Previous validation studies support the appropriateness of this strategy 12–14. For example, Wang et al. (2023) demonstrated that iBEAT V2.0, a deep learning-based pipeline optimized for infant cortical reconstruction, produces accurate and reproducible surfaces across scanners and imaging protocols 12. Similarly, Makropoulos et al. (2018) established a neonatal minimal processing pipeline designed to capture the unique anatomical features of early development 13. For older participants, the widely adopted Human Connectome Project pipeline and FreeSurfer have been rigorously validated in multisite settings and are considered standards for adult cortical surface analysis 14.
By using pipelines tailored to the anatomical characteristics of each age group, we aimed to minimize reconstruction errors and enhance the reliability of cortical thickness estimation across the lifespan. All subsequent analyses were conducted on surfaces registered to a common template space, further mitigating concerns about cross-pipeline inconsistency. We have rephrased the relevant sections in the Supplementary Methods section (page 2):
“This age-appropriate pipeline selection minimizes cortical reconstruction bias across the lifespan, and all surfaces were subsequently registered to a common template to ensure cross-pipeline comparability.”
Q1.20 The fMRI data is not necessarily scanned under the same condition, even in the lifespan HCP datasets. For example, the BCP data for the first three years are scanned with the children asleep. How is this discrepancy handled to ensure the validity of findings?
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. Indeed, scanning conditions necessarily vary across lifespan datasets due to practical and ethical considerations. For example, in the Baby Connectome Project (BCP), infants aged 0-35 months were typically scanned during natural sleep, whereas older children could be scanned either awake or asleep depending on feasibility 15. Similarly, in the Developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP), virtually all infants were scanned during natural sleep. In contrast, large-scale adolescent and adult cohorts such as ABCD, HCP, ADNI, CamCAN, and UK Biobank explicitly required participants to remain awake during resting-state scans (eyes open or eyes closed, depending on protocol). Unfortunately, precise per-scan records of sleep/awake state are not publicly available for dHCP and BCP, preventing direct stratification by brain state.
We fully acknowledge that brain state can influence functional activity patterns 16 and may affect gradient estimation. However, several factors mitigate this concern. First, the gradients observed show robust and biologically plausible age-related trajectories that are consistent across datasets and scales, suggesting that they are not solely driven by state differences. Second, all datasets underwent harmonized preprocessing pipelines, which help minimize systematic biases. Third, the vary large sample size provides statistical stability, reducing the influence of individual-level variation in scan conditions. We now explicitly note this as a limitation in the revised manuscript (page 21):
“Finally, the large fMRI datasets exhibited heterogeneity in scanning states: neonate and infant data were primarily acquired during natural sleep, whereas children and adults were scanned during wakefulness. Given differences in functional brain activity between sleep and wake states 73, we cannot rule out the potential influence of this acquisition discrepancy on the observed patterns. Future studies that control for this variable by using identical scanning states across age groups will be important to clarify this issue.”
Q1.21 Phase I ends at one month postnatally, and Phase III begins at age five. These timepoints coincide with the end of the dHCP and the end of the BCP, respectively. The dHCP, BCP, and the remaining lifespan HCP studies use different imaging protocols. Therefore, it is likely that the demarcation of Phases I, II, and III might be an artifact of differences in image acquisition.
R: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this point. To assess whether the phase boundaries coinciding with the transitions between the dHCP, BCP, and HCP datasets could be driven by differences in acquisition protocols, we explicitly evaluated the potential influence of such site and protocol effects. A single harmonization across the entire lifespan would not be appropriate in this context, as the topographic architecture of functional connectivity systematically changes with age. Applying one global harmonization procedure could inadvertently distort age-specific topographic features or impose artificial similarity across distinct developmental stages.
Instead, we minimized acquisition-related variability by removing site-specific effects within each age group before gradient estimation. Specifically, for each age group, site was modeled as a random effect in the vertex-wise FC data and regressed out prior to constructing group-level connectivity matrices and computing gradients. When gradients and clustering were derived from these within-age-group-harmonized data, the same three developmental phases (early anterior-posterior differentiation; emergence of the S-A axis in early childhood; and subsequent expansion, refinement, and stabilization) were reproduced and closely matched the results reported in the main text. Moreover, when determining optimal number of clusters, both 3- and 4-cluster solutions were identified with equal frequency across clustering indices. We reported the 3-cluster solution in the main text, while the 4-cluster solution only further subdivided the earliest phase (32w to 3 months). This concordance indicates that the observed phase boundaries reflect genuine developmental transitions rather than artifacts arising from dataset boundaries or acquisition differences. We have added a corresponding description in the revised Results (page 7) and Supplementary Results (page 3):
Results: “The three developmental phases were also identified through both individual-level gradient clustering without predefined age bins and within-age-group-harmonized analysis (Supplementary Fig. 3, 4). This indicates that the observed patterns were robust and not driven by specific age-grouping schemes or site related confounds.”
Supplementary Results: “To ensure that the phase boundaries were not artifacts of differences in acquisition protocols across datasets, site was modeled as random effect and regressed out within each age group prior to computing group-level connectivity matrices and gradients. Analyses using these harmonized data reproduced the same three phases, indicating that the observed phase boundaries reflect genuine developmental transitions rather than dataset or acquisition differences (Supplementary Fig. 4).”

Q1.22 How is longitudinal information, repeated observations of each subject, dealt with? Not doing so might bias the results.
R: To minimize potential bias introduced by repeated measurements from the same participants, we restricted our analyses to a single imaging session per individual across all longitudinal datasets. This ensure that each participant contributed only once to the cross-sectional lifespan analyses, thereby preventing inflated sample sizes or undue weighting of individuals with repeated scans. This procedure is described in the Methods section of the revised manuscript (page 22):
“For participants with multiple imaging sessions, only the first scan was selected for inclusion, ensuring that each individual contributed a single observation to the analyses.”
Q1.23 The effects of sex may vary nonlinearly across age, especially given the long developmental time span covered in this study. However, this nonlinearity does not appear to have been modeled.
R: To test whether the effects of sex on gradient measures vary nonlinearly across the lifespan, in the revised manuscript we performed additional analyses at the global, system, and regional levels.
Specifically, we used the GAMLSS framework, which flexibly captures nonlinear trajectories across age. Two nested models were compared: a baseline model including main effects of age and sex, and a full model including an age-by-sex interaction term. Both models controlled for mean FD as a covariate, and site was modeled as a random effect. Significance of the interaction was assessed using the generalized likelihood ratio tests (GLRT), with FDR correction applied (q < 0.05).
At the global level, females showed significantly higher explanation ratio, gradient range, and variation compared with males across the lifespan (all p<0.05, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 35a). At the system level, the overall hierarchical organization was preserved, with the default-mode and frontoparietal systems consistently showed higher gradient ranges and standard deviations, while the sensorimotor system displayed lower values throughout life. Importantly, females exhibited significantly greater gradient ranges and variations than males (all p<0.001, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 35b). Moreover, peak age analyses revealed that in several functional systems, including visual, limbic, frontoparietal, and default mode networks, females demonstrated significantly later maturational peaks than males (all p<0.001, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 35c & Supplementary Table 8), suggesting delayed maturational timing in females. At the regional level, females exhibited higher gradient values in temporal, precuneus, medial prefrontal and somatomotor regions, whereas males showed higher values in occipital and lateral prefrontal regions (p<0.001, FDR-corrected; Supplementary Fig. 35d).
These findings have been incorporated into the Supplementary Methods (page 3) and Results sections (page 7):
Supplementary Methods:
“To test whether the effects of sex on gradient measures vary nonlinearly across the lifespan, we performed additional analyses at the global, system, and regional levels. Specifically, we used the GAMLSS framework, which flexibly captures nonlinear trajectories across age. Two nested models were compared: a baseline model including main effects of age and sex, and a full model including an age-by-sex interaction term. Both models, controlled for mean FD as a covariate, and site was modeled as a random effect. Significance of the interaction was assessed by comparing the model fits of the baseline and full models using the generalized likelihood ratio test (GLRT). All p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons using the FDR (q < 0.05). The direction of sex differences was determined based on the mean differences between the fitted sex-specific growth curves.”
